Topic: generative-and-multimodal

Models that generate images, video and audio, and models that see and read, taught from zero: autoencoders and latents, diffusion and flow matching, latent diffusion and diffusion transformers, vision encoders, vision-language models, native multimodal models, and how to evaluate all of them. Small models trained on an Apple M1 Pro, larger open models run for inference, published results kept apart. Data as of October 2026.
0 One screen1 Families2 Latents3 Diffusion and flow4 Latent diffusion, DiT5 Vision encoders6 VLMs7 Native multimodal8 Video and audio9 Evaluation10 ChoosingMistakesInterviewChild pages

A generative model learns what its training data looks like well enough to produce new examples of it: new images, video, sound or text that could plausibly have come from the same source. A multimodal model takes in or produces more than one kind of data (images and text, video and audio). This topic covers both, taught from zero: how images are compressed into latents, how diffusion and flow models turn random noise into an image, how a model "sees" an image as a sequence of patches, and how a language model is taught to read those patches. Reading time about 30 minutes (measured from the words outside widgets at 200 a minute; the folded answers add about 10).

The whole subject on one screen: five ways to generate, three ways to understand

Understanding, not generating. A vision encoder turns an image into vectors (ViT, CLIP, SigLIP). A vision-language model (VLM) feeds those vectors to a language model, which answers in text. A native multimodal model puts text and image tokens into one transformer, which can read and write both.

What ties them together. Modern generators work in a compressed latent (section 2), read images as patches with a transformer (sections 4, 5), and get text through an encoder trained on image-caption pairs (section 5).

Sources for each cell are in the section the family name links to.

Each section ends with its lab tab, its child page and the existing pages that already derive the maths: Variational inference and generative-model maths (ELBO, VAEs, diffusion, scores, guidance, flow matching) and the paper pages for DDPM, latent diffusion, ViT and CLIP. This page links them rather than repeating them.

1. What a generative model is, and the five families

The problem. A 28 × 28 greyscale image is a list of 784 numbers, a point in a 784-dimensional space. Almost every point in that space is static; the images that look like clothing occupy a tiny, oddly shaped region of it. We never get a formula for that region, only examples from it (the training set). We call the unknown rule that produced the examples the data distribution, written p(x). A generative model is a recipe for drawing new points from (an approximation of) that region. Some families can also score a given image, reporting how probable the model finds it (its likelihood); others can only sample. A conditional model draws from p(x | c), where the condition c is a class label or a text prompt.

Every pixel depends on many others (a sleeve on the left implies one on the right); the five families are five ways to capture that, and differ mostly in network calls per sample and training signal.

Autoregressive. Write the image as a sequence and predict each element from the ones before: p(x) = ∏ p(xi | x<i), a language model's chain rule and cross-entropy loss, with exact likelihood. Raw pixels gave poor samples (Gated PixelCNN: FID 65.93 on CIFAR-10, DDPM Table 1); learned image tokens (section 2) worked better: Parti treats text-to-image "as a sequence-to-sequence modeling problem" at 20B parameters (Yu et al. 2022). Cost: one call per token, in order.

VAE (variational autoencoder, Kingma and Welling, Dec 2013). Encode an image to a short code kept close to a standard Gaussian, decode it back; a random Gaussian code then decodes to something sensible. One call per sample, but blurry (section 2).

GAN (generative adversarial network, Goodfellow et al., June 2014). A generator turns noise into an image; a discriminator tries to tell its images from real ones; "the training procedure for G is to maximize the probability of D making a mistake". Sharp images in one call, but no likelihood, notoriously unstable training, and mode collapse: the generator finds a few outputs that fool the judge and stops covering the rest of the data.

Diffusion (Ho et al., June 2020). Destroy training images by adding Gaussian noise in many small steps, and train a network to undo one step. To generate, start from pure noise and apply the network again and again. DDPM reached FID 3.17 on CIFAR-10, the best unconditional score in its table (DDPM page).

Flow matching (Lipman et al. 2022; rectified flow, Liu et al. 2022). Learn a velocity field that carries noise to data along nearly straight paths; generate by following it. Straighter paths need fewer steps.

One image, made three ways: count the network calls

One Fashion-MNIST pullover made by an autoregressive model (49 tokens, one call each), a diffusion sampler (50 steps) and a flow sampler (8 Euler steps). Each frame is the exact path a sampler follows when its model already knows the answer, not a trained model's guess (those are in the Diffusion lab and Flow lab). The chart shows image against noise share: diffusion curves, flow goes straight.

Autoregressive

Predict: a 512 × 512 image as Chameleon tokens (1,024 per image) or as 30 steps of a diffusion sampler with guidance. Which needs more sequential network calls?
derived Autoregressive: 1,024 calls, one per token, each waiting for the last (Chameleon encodes "a 512×512 image into 1024 discrete tokens from a codebook of size 8192", Chameleon Team 2024). Diffusion: 30 steps × 2 (conditional and unconditional pass) = 60 calls, and diffusers runs the two passes of a step as one batch of 2 (torch.cat([latents] * 2), pipeline_stable_diffusion.py line 1037, v0.41.0), so 30 sequential rounds; 1,024 / 60 ≈ 17. But each autoregressive call reuses a cache and processes one new token, while each diffusion call processes the whole image: counting calls alone is not counting compute (section 10).

2. Latents: generate something smaller than the image

The problem. Pixels are expensive and redundant. A 512 × 512 colour image is 786,432 numbers, most of them describing texture the eye barely registers, and a diffusion model pays for every one of them at every step. The fix that every modern image and video generator uses is to generate a compressed version instead, a latent, and turn it back into pixels once at the end.

Predict: Stable Diffusion v1 works on a 64 × 64 grid with 4 channels for a 512 × 512 RGB image. How many times fewer numbers does each denoising step handle?
derived 512 × 512 × 3 = 786,432 against 64 × 64 × 4 = 16,384: 48 times. The spatial grid shrinks 64 times (8 per side, the "downsampling-factor 8 autoencoder" of the Stable Diffusion README), but each position keeps 4 channels instead of 3. The LDM paper measured at least 2.7 times faster training and sampling at a milder 4 per side (LDM page, Table 6).

Autoencoder. An encoder network maps the image to a small code (the bottleneck); a decoder maps the code back; training minimises the reconstruction loss, the difference between input and output. A plain autoencoder compresses well but does not generate: its codes land wherever training put them, so a random code falls in a gap and decodes to nonsense. TODO (Latent lab): samples from random codes, plain autoencoder against VAE, on the running example.

VAE. The variational autoencoder's encoder outputs a mean and a spread for each code dimension, training samples the code from that range (the reparameterisation trick, z = μ + σ · ε, lets gradients pass through the sampling), and a KL penalty pulls every image's range towards a standard Gaussian. The space fills in, so a random Gaussian code decodes to something plausible. The price is blur: with a squared-error reconstruction loss, the best guess for detail the code cannot pin down is the average of the possibilities, and an average of sharp images is a blurry one. A weight β on the KL term trades the two: more β, a smoother space and blurrier pictures. TODO (Latent lab): the beta sweep on the running example (reconstruction error and sample quality at each beta).

VQ-VAE and image tokens. Replace the continuous code by the nearest entry of a learned codebook (van den Oord et al. 2017): the image becomes a grid of integers, image tokens, that a transformer can predict like words. A commitment loss keeps encoder and codebook together; the classic failure is codebook collapse, most entries never used.

The Stable Diffusion autoencoder is a VAE in name, but its KL weight is about 10−6 and it is trained with a perceptual loss (distance between deep-network features, LPIPS) plus a patch adversarial loss (a small GAN judge on image patches), which together avoid the blur of pixel losses (LDM page, Stage 1). Its latents are not unit-variance, so every Stable Diffusion v1 pipeline multiplies them by a scaling factor of 0.18215 before diffusion and divides by it before decoding (v1 config); later models use 16 channels and their own factors (FLUX: 0.3611, FLUX code). Forget the factor and the denoiser sees a signal about 5.5 times too large (1 / 0.18215, derived), so its noise schedule no longer matches. TODO (Latent lab): the fixed test images through the SD VAE: reconstruction error, and what happens without the scaling factor.

3. Diffusion and flow matching, side by side

Diffusion in four sentences. The forward process mixes an image x0 with Gaussian noise ε: xt = √āt x0 + √(1 − āt) ε, with āt falling from 1 to almost 0 over T steps (1,000 in DDPM); the noise schedule sets how fast, and the signal-to-noise ratio āt / (1 − āt) compares schedules. Training picks an image, a random t and noise, and asks the denoiser network to predict the noise from xt, with a squared error. Sampling starts from pure noise and removes the predicted noise a little at a time; the rule per step is the sampler. The network may instead predict the clean image or a mix called v (Salimans and Ho 2022), which changes which noise levels the loss emphasises.

Samplers and steps. DDPM's own sampler adds fresh noise at every step and needs hundreds to a thousand. DDIM (Song, Meng and Ermon 2020) makes sampling deterministic and works in 10 to 50; higher-order ODE solvers such as DPM-Solver (Lu et al. 2022) cut that further. Fewer steps means fewer network calls, and too few means blurred or broken samples. TODO (Diffusion lab): the same noise through 1, 4, 10, 50 and 250 steps with DDPM and DDIM on the tiny model, and on Stable Diffusion v1.5 (quality and seconds per step, measured on Apple M1 Pro).

Classifier-free guidance (CFG, Ho and Salimans 2022) makes the model follow its prompt harder. Train with the prompt dropped some of the time, so one network predicts both with and without it; at sampling, run both and push past the conditional prediction: ε = εuncond + w (εcond − εuncond). It doubles the calls per step, and large w buys prompt fidelity at the cost of variety and, at the extreme, over-saturated colours. Hugging Face diffusers' Stable Diffusion pipeline defaults to num_inference_steps = 50 and guidance_scale = 7.5 (pipeline_stable_diffusion.py lines 785 and 788, v0.41.0), and applies the formula above at line 1055; the math page, section 17 derives it and shows the diversity loss on a toy. TODO (Diffusion lab): one prompt at guidance 0 to 10 on Stable Diffusion v1.5.

Flow matching in three sentences. Pair each image with a noise sample and draw the straight line between them, xt = (1 − t) x0 + t ε; train a network to predict the direction of that line, ε − x0 (the velocity), from xt and t, with a squared-error loss. To generate, start at noise and step against the predicted velocity with an ODE solver (Euler: move by velocity × step size). If the learned paths were exactly straight, one step would land on the image; they bend because one noise sample could lead to many images, and reflow (retraining on the model's own noise-image pairs, Liu, Gong and Liu 2022) straightens them.

Diffusion (DDPM-style)Flow matching (rectified flow)
Path from data to noiseVariance-preserving curve set by the scheduleStraight line
Network predictsNoise (or clean image, or v)Velocity ε − x0
SamplingDDPM (stochastic, many steps), DDIM or solvers (10 to 50)ODE solver, usually Euler; few steps; 1 to 4 when distilled
GuidanceCFGCFG, or guidance distilled into the model
Used byDDPM, Stable Diffusion 1 and 2, SDXL, ImagenStable Diffusion 3, FLUX.1, Movie Gen

They are one family. Flow matching "is compatible with a general family of Gaussian probability paths", "which subsumes existing diffusion paths as specific instances", and straight paths "are more efficient than diffusion paths" (Lipman et al. 2022); a trained diffusion model also defines an ODE, the probability-flow ODE that DDIM and the solvers integrate (Song et al. 2021). So the choice is mostly the path, the prediction target and how training weights the noise levels; Stable Diffusion 3 changed the last, biasing training noise "towards perceptually relevant scales" (Esser et al. 2024).

Few-step generation. Distillation trains a student to jump several steps at once: progressive distillation halves the step count repeatedly (Salimans and Ho 2022), consistency models map any point on the path to its end (Song et al. 2023), and adversarial diffusion distillation samples "in just 1-4 steps" (Sauer et al. 2023), as FLUX.1 [schnell] does vendor (model card). The usual price is some variety and fine detail. 4. Latent diffusion and diffusion transformers: a text-to-image system

A text-to-image model is three networks in a row. Stable Diffusion v1, the first widely used open one, is the cleanest example:

Text encoderPrompt to 77 token vectorsfrozen CLIP ViT-L/14 text tower, 123M parameters
▶
DenoiserRuns once per step on the 64 × 64 × 4 latent, reading the text through cross-attentionU-Net, 860M parameters
▶
VAE decoderLatent to 512 × 512 pixels, oncef = 8, 4 channels, scale 0.18215

Sizes from the CompVis README ("its 860M UNet and 123M text encoder") vendor; 77 tokens is the context length of CLIP's tokenizer (clip.py). TODO (Latent or Diffusion lab): parameter counts of the three components of the pinned Stable Diffusion v1.5 checkpoint, counted from its weights.

Conditioning. In cross-attention the latent's positions are queries and the text tokens keys and values, so each region looks up the words that concern it (the LDM page covers it and the add-ons built on it: ControlNet, IP-Adapter, LoRA). The text encoder matters more than its size suggests: Imagen found that "increasing the size of the language model in Imagen boosts both sample fidelity and image-text alignment" far more than enlarging the diffusion model (Saharia et al. 2022), and Stable Diffusion 3 credits its joint text-image transformer with better "typography", spelling words inside the image.

From U-Net to transformer. The U-Net is a convolutional network that shrinks the latent through several resolutions and grows it back, with skip connections between matching levels. A diffusion transformer (DiT, Peebles and Xie, Dec 2022) cuts the latent into patches and runs a plain transformer; more compute per step "consistently" gave lower FID, reaching 2.27 on ImageNet 256 × 256 (a 32 × 32 × 4 latent in patches of 2 is 256 tokens, derived). Stable Diffusion 3's MMDiT puts text and image tokens in one sequence with "separate weights for the two modalities" (Esser et al. 2024); FLUX.1 is "a 12 billion parameter rectified flow transformer" (model card).

What one image costs. Text encoder once (twice with guidance: diffusers also encodes the empty or negative prompt, line 454), denoiser once per step and twice with guidance (run as one batch of two, line 1037), decoder once (line 1085, after dividing by the scaling factor). With 50 steps and guidance, that is 100 denoiser evaluations against one decode, so the denoiser is almost the whole bill, and steps × (1 or 2) is the number to cut. TODO (Diffusion lab): Stable Diffusion v1.5 seconds per step and per decode in fp16 on the M1 Pro's GPU, measured.

5. Vision encoders: how a model sees

Images as patches. A transformer reads a sequence, so the Vision Transformer (ViT, Dosovitskiy et al., Oct 2020) cuts the image into a grid of square patches, flattens each (a 16 × 16 RGB patch is 768 numbers), multiplies it by one learned matrix (the patch embedding) and adds a learned position embedding saying where the patch came from. A 224 × 224 image in patches of 16 is 14 × 14 = 196 tokens derived. The output is either an extra summary token prepended to the sequence ([CLS]) or an average over all patch outputs. A convolutional network builds in the assumptions that nearby pixels matter together and that a pattern means the same thing anywhere (its inductive bias); a ViT has to learn them from data, and beat the best CNNs of 2020 only after pre-training on 300M images (ViT page).

Learning without labels. Self-supervised methods train on images alone: MAE hides most patches ("e.g., 75%") and fills them in (He et al. 2021); DINO-style methods match a slowly updated copy of the network across crops (DINOv2); both are on Contrastive and self-supervised learning.

Learning from captions: CLIP. CLIP (Radford et al., Feb 2021) trains an image encoder and a text encoder together on 400M web image-caption pairs. In a batch of N pairs it computes all N × N image-text similarities and applies a softmax cross-entropy along each row and column so that each image picks out its own caption and vice versa (the contrastive or InfoNCE loss), with a learned temperature that sharpens the softmax. The payoff is zero-shot classification: embed "a photo of a dog", "a photo of a cat" and so on, and pick the class whose text is nearest the image, with no task-specific training; CLIP's best model reached 76.2% on ImageNet that way (CLIP page). Its text tower became Stable Diffusion's text encoder (section 4) and its image tower the eyes of the first VLMs (section 6).

SigLIP. The softmax needs every similarity in the batch, which makes huge batches expensive to shard. SigLIP (Zhai et al. 2023) scores each pair independently with a sigmoid, which "does not require a global view of the pairwise similarities for normalization", works better at small batches and scales to larger ones (84.5% zero-shot ImageNet with locked image features, four TPUv4 chips, two days vendor). SigLIP-family towers sit in many open VLMs, SmolVLM's included.

What the embeddings miss. A contrastive embedding keeps what helps match captions and drops much else. CLIP reads text in images so well that a handwritten label can override the object: OpenAI called these typographic attacks, noting they need "no more technology than pen and paper" (OpenAI, March 2021, archived). Such models also handle word order, counting and spatial relations poorly, behaving partly like bags of words (Yuksekgonul et al. 2022). TODO (Vision lab): zero-shot accuracy of CLIP and SigLIP 2 on the small labelled set, and the typographic-attack probe, measured.

6. Vision-language models: teaching a language model to read images

The recipe. A VLM bolts a vision encoder onto a pretrained language model. In LLaVA (Liu et al., Apr 2023), the pattern most open models follow, the encoder turns the image into patch vectors, a small projector (one linear layer; a two-layer MLP in LLaVA-1.5) maps each into the language model's embedding space, and these image tokens replace an image placeholder in the prompt, attended to like words. The alternative is cross-attention: Flamingo kept a pretrained vision model and a 70B language model frozen and trained new layers between them, "an 80B parameter VLM" (DeepMind, April 2022), whose open reproduction is named for "Interleaved Cross-attention" (IDEFICS). Cross-attention keeps images out of the context window; tokens are simpler, and most open VLMs since 2023 use them.

Imagepixels, maybe tiled into crops
▶
Vision encoderone vector per patchCLIP or SigLIP ViT
▶
Projectormerge and map into the LLM's spacelinear or MLP; optional token merging
▶
Language modelreads image tokens and text, writes text

How many tokens is an image? It is the patch count after any merging: LLaVA-1.5's CLIP ViT-L/14 at 336 pixels gives (336 / 14)2 = 576 tokens per image derived, as many as a page of text. Higher resolution helps reading small text but costs tokens quadratically, so models tile a large image into crops plus a thumbnail, process images at their own resolution (Qwen2-VL's "Naive Dynamic Resolution", Wang et al. 2024), or merge neighbouring patch vectors before the projector (pixel shuffle, trading spatial positions for channels). TODO (VLM lab): SmolVLM's token count for the fixed test images at several resolutions, and the exact prompt its processor builds.

Training in stages. LLaVA first trains only the projector on 595K image-caption pairs, encoder and language model frozen, so image vectors land where the language model can read them; then projector and language model together on instruction conversations that a text-only GPT-4 wrote from captions and object boxes (LLaVA, section 4.2). LLaVA-1.5 used "merely 1.2M publicly available data" and "~1 day on a single 8-A100 node" (Liu et al. 2023). Later recipes change data, resolution and what is frozen, but keep align-then-instruct.

Failure modes. The best known is object hallucination: naming things that are not in the image, especially objects that usually co-occur with what is there. POPE measures it with yes/no questions about present and absent objects (Li et al. 2023). Counting, small text and left-right relations are the other usual errors. TODO (VLM lab): accuracy on the small question set, the hallucination probe (yes rate on absent objects) and seconds per image, measured.

7. Native multimodal models: one transformer for both

A VLM reads images but writes only text. A native (or unified) multimodal model reads and writes both with one network. Three designs are published:

  • Everything is a token (early fusion). Chameleon (Chameleon Team, May 2024) turns each 512 × 512 image into 1,024 tokens from a codebook of 8,192 and trains one 7B or 34B transformer on interleaved text and image tokens; generating an image is next-token prediction. Simple, but slow (section 1's drill) and capped by the tokenizer's detail.
  • Two encodings, one transformer. Janus argues that understanding and generation want different image representations and "decouple[s] visual encoding into separate pathways" while keeping "a single, unified transformer" (Wu et al., Oct 2024).
  • Two objectives, one transformer. Transfusion "combines the language modeling loss function (next token prediction) with diffusion" in one model, up to 7B parameters on 2T tokens, with images as continuous latent patches rather than discrete tokens (Zhou et al., Aug 2024).

The closed frontier publishes little. OpenAI's system card for GPT-4o image generation says only: "Unlike DALL·E, which operates as a diffusion model, 4o image generation is an autoregressive model natively embedded within ChatGPT" (OpenAI, 25 March 2025, archived) vendor; tokenizer, decoder and sizes are not disclosed. The traffic also runs the other way: diffusion is now used to generate text, as on DiffusionGemma Technical Report.

Go deeper (optional): child page Native multimodal models; every unified model with its date and licence in the Model map.

8. Video and audio, in brief

Video is latent diffusion or flow with time added: the autoencoder compresses space and time, and a transformer denoises spacetime patches. Sora is "trained on and subsequently generates videos within this compressed latent space" (OpenAI, Feb 2024, archived) vendor; Movie Gen is a 30B-parameter transformer trained with flow matching (Polyak et al. 2024). Every frame adds patches and attention grows with the square of the total, so video compresses time too and costs far more than an image. The hard failures are temporal: objects changing identity or vanishing between frames, physics that does not hold.

Audio follows two routes. A neural audio codec turns the waveform into parallel streams of discrete tokens that a language model predicts: AudioLM "maps the input audio to a sequence of discrete tokens" (Borsos et al. 2022), MusicGen uses one "single-stage transformer LM together with efficient token interleaving patterns" (Copet et al. 2023). Or diffusion generates a continuous audio latent, as in Stable Audio (Evans et al. 2024).

9. Evaluation: what the numbers measure and how they mislead

FID (Fréchet Inception Distance, Heusel et al. 2017) is the standard score for generated images. Pass a set of real images and a set of generated ones through Inception-v3, an ImageNet classifier, and keep one 2,048-number feature vector per image; fit a Gaussian (mean and covariance) to each set; report the distance between the two Gaussians, ‖μr − μg‖2 + Tr(Σr + Σg − 2(ΣrΣg)1/2). Lower is better, and it penalises both bad images and too little variety. Its pitfalls are well documented:

  • Sample count. The estimate is biased upwards at small counts ("inconsistent results when varying the sample size", Jayasumana et al.), so compare only at equal counts (50,000 by convention). FID of real images against real images at several sample counts is measured in the setup (fid_floor.json). The child page Evaluating generative models repeats this for every metric at six sample counts (its own draws, real against real: FID 2.538 at 10,000; 15.9, 27.8 and 44.9 at 1,000, 500 and 250 measured).
  • Preprocessing. Resizing and JPEG compression "can induce large variations"; aliased resizing corrupts the features, and "FID can actually improve if the generated images are also subsequently compressed" (Parmar, Zhang and Zhu 2021, the clean-fid paper).
  • ImageNet leakage. Inception's features are so tied to ImageNet classes that matching the class histogram of the real set lowers FID "without any real gain in image quality" (Kynkäänniemi et al. 2022).
  • Wrong features for modern content. For text-to-image models FID "contradicts human raters"; CMMD, a kernel distance on CLIP embeddings, is one proposed fix (Jayasumana et al.).
  • One number for two things. Precision (are samples realistic?) and recall (is the data's variety covered?) separate fidelity from diversity (Kynkäänniemi et al. 2019). Papers rarely give FID error bars; differences under about 0.5 between single runs are not evidence (LDM page).

Prompt alignment. CLIPScore is the CLIP similarity between an image and its prompt (Hessel et al. 2021); it inherits CLIP's blindness to counts and relations (section 5). GenEval instead runs an object detector to check "object co-occurrence, position, count, and color" against the prompt (Ghosh et al. 2023). The kind of failure it catches: Stable Diffusion v1.5 asked for "an astronaut riding a horse on the moon" drew the astronaut on the moon and no horse measured (setup smoke test, seed 5), an image a global similarity score can still rate as close to its prompt. Human preference remains the final judge: pairwise votes on text-to-image and vision arenas, with the same caveats as text arenas (style, self-selected prompts, vendors testing private variants), are covered on Human preference and arenas.

VLMs are scored on question-answering benchmarks (MMMU, MathVista, ChartQA, DocVQA and others, on Long-context and multimodal benchmarks). Many questions can be answered without the image (Chen et al. 2024), so report a text-only baseline beside every score, and probe absent objects directly (section 6).

Predict: two teams report FID 9.1 and 8.4 for their models. What do you need to know before believing the second is better?
All of them. Sample count biases the score, resizing and compression "can induce large variations" (clean-fid), the reference set (training or held-out images, how many) changes it, and two implementations differ (the LDM paper reports 7.76 against 7.77 for the same samples). A 0.7 gap between single runs computed differently says nothing; recompute both with one tool on the same reference set, and look at precision and recall and at images.

What one text-to-image sample costs, counted

Go deeper (optional): the trade-offs per child page are listed at the end of this tab; serving costs in general (batching, quantisation, GPUs) are on Topic: inference-and-serving.

Common mistakes

Decoding latents without the VAE's scaling factor, or with another model's

Stable Diffusion v1 latents are multiplied by 0.18215 before diffusion and divided by it before decoding; each later autoencoder has its own factor (FLUX's 16-channel one uses 0.3611). Skip it and the denoiser sees latents about 5.5 times too large, so its noise schedule is wrong for them; use another model's and the decoder gets the wrong scale. Read it from the loaded model (vae.config.scaling_factor), never from memory, and check where it came from: the pinned Stable Diffusion v1.5 vae/config.json has no scaling_factor entry at all, so diffusers silently falls back to its class default of 0.18215 (autoencoder_kl.py line 90, v0.41.0), which is right for this checkpoint and wrong for any other autoencoder saved the same way (section 2). TODO (Latent lab): the measured effect on the fixed test images.

Comparing FIDs computed at different sample counts or with different code

FID is biased upwards at small sample counts, and resizing, compression and the reference set move it (section 9). Two samples drawn from the same distribution still get a positive FID, and it shrinks as the count grows: 

import numpy as np
from scipy import linalg

def fid(a, b):  # the Frechet distance FID uses, on any features
    m1, m2 = a.mean(0), b.mean(0)
    s1, s2 = np.cov(a, rowvar=False), np.cov(b, rowvar=False)
    covmean = linalg.sqrtm(s1 @ s2).real
    return float(((m1 - m2) ** 2).sum() + np.trace(s1 + s2 - 2 * covmean))

d = 64                                   # Inception features have 2,048 dimensions; 64 keeps this fast
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
A = rng.normal(size=(d, d)) / np.sqrt(d)
cov = A @ A.T + 0.1 * np.eye(d)          # one fixed "true" feature distribution
L = np.linalg.cholesky(cov)
draw = lambda n: rng.normal(size=(n, d)) @ L.T

for n in [500, 2000, 10000, 50000]:
    scores = [fid(draw(n), draw(n)) for _ in range(3)]
    print(f"n = {n:>6}: FID between two samples of the SAME distribution = {np.mean(scores):.4f} (3 draws: {', '.join(f'{s:.4f}' for s in scores)})")
n =    500: FID between two samples of the SAME distribution = 3.3324 (3 draws: 3.3952, 3.3297, 3.2723)
n =   2000: FID between two samples of the SAME distribution = 0.8557 (3 draws: 0.8410, 0.8715, 0.8546)
n =  10000: FID between two samples of the SAME distribution = 0.1669 (3 draws: 0.1666, 0.1617, 0.1726)
n =  50000: FID between two samples of the SAME distribution = 0.0331 (3 draws: 0.0338, 0.0334, 0.0322)

measured on Apple M1 Pro CPU (numpy 2.5.4, scipy 1.18.1; src/read/fid_bias.py). The true distance is 0; the estimate falls roughly as 1 / n, and with 2,048 Inception dimensions instead of 64 the bias is far larger. So "FID 3.3" at 500 samples and "FID 0.03" at 50,000 can be the same model: compare only at equal n, and prefer 50,000.

Mixing up the two guidance-scale conventions

The paper writes ε = (1 + w) εcond − w εuncond; libraries write εuncond + s(εcond − εuncond), so s = 1 + w, and "guidance 7.5" in diffusers is w = 6.5 (math page, section 17). Scale 1 in the library convention means no guidance at all.

A scheduler that does not match how the model was trained

The sampler must know what the network predicts (noise, clean image or v), which way time runs (diffusion papers put data at t = 0; Lipman et al.'s flow matching puts noise there) and the training schedule. A mismatch still produces images, just bad ones: washed out, noisy or over-contrasted. In diffusers the scheduler's prediction_type and schedule come from the checkpoint's scheduler/scheduler_config.json; swap samplers with from_config so they inherit it.

Training on images in [0, 1] (or [0, 255])

The forward process assumes data on the scale of unit-variance noise: DDPM scales pixel values "linearly to [−1, 1]" (Ho et al. 2020, section 3.3). Unscaled data changes the effective signal-to-noise ratio at every timestep; samples look grey or blown out. Clip predicted clean images to the data range while sampling.

Counting steps instead of network passes

Guidance doubles the passes per step; some solvers make two passes per step (Heun's method, as in EDM). Compare samplers and models by passes (and by time on the same hardware), not by the step count printed in a config (section 10).

Reading CLIPScore as image quality

It measures agreement with the prompt as CLIP sees it: a sharp image and a mushy one with the right objects score alike, and CLIP cannot count or check relations (section 5). Pair it with a fidelity metric, GenEval-style checks and human preference.

Judging a VLM by its captions

Fluent captions hide hallucination. Ask yes/no questions about objects that are absent as well as present (POPE), report the yes rate on absent objects, and run a text-only baseline with the image removed: questions it still answers are not testing vision (section 9).

Shrinking the image until the text is unreadable

A VLM's processor resizes or tiles the image to fit a token budget. Small text that falls below a patch or two is gone before the language model sees it; raise the resolution or the tile count, and watch the token count and the context it uses (section 6).

Interview questions

Short answers; answer first, then open. The design questions have no single right answer: name the constraint that decides it.

Why are VAE samples blurry, and why is Stable Diffusion's autoencoder sharp?
A Gaussian (squared-error) reconstruction loss is minimised by the mean of the images consistent with the code, and the mean of several sharp images is blurry; the KL term forces codes to overlap, which leaves more of them ambiguous. Stable Diffusion's autoencoder barely regularises the latent (KL weight about 10−6) and adds a perceptual loss and a patch adversarial loss, which reward realistic texture over the average. It is a compressor, not a generator: the diffusion model does the generating.
Explain diffusion training and sampling in one minute.
Training: take an image, pick a random noise level, mix in that much Gaussian noise with the closed form xt = √āt x0 + √(1 − āt) ε, and train a network to predict the noise with a squared error. Sampling: start from pure noise and repeatedly use the predicted noise to step to a slightly less noisy image, 20 to 50 times with a deterministic sampler. The network never generates in one go; it only ever denoises a little.
Diffusion against flow matching: what is actually different?
The path from noise to data (a variance-preserving curve against a straight line), what the network predicts (noise against velocity) and how training weights the noise levels. Both define an ODE that is integrated at sampling, and Gaussian diffusion paths are a special case of flow matching. Straight paths are easier to integrate with large steps, so flow models need fewer steps and distil well to 1 to 4.
What is classifier-free guidance, what does it cost, and what goes wrong at high scale?
Train one network with and without the condition (drop it some of the time); at sampling extrapolate from the unconditional prediction through the conditional one. It costs a second pass per step (2× compute, though batched). Too high a scale over-saturates colours, reduces variety and pushes samples off the data; a little guidance also rescues too-short samplers. Distilled models often fold guidance in and run one pass.
How does an image become tokens in a VLM, and how many?
A ViT encoder cuts the image into patches (14 or 16 pixels) and outputs one vector per patch; a projector (linear or MLP) maps them into the language model's embedding space, often after merging neighbours; they replace an image placeholder in the prompt. Count = (side / patch)2 per tile, divided by any merge factor, times the number of tiles: LLaVA-1.5 at 336 pixels and patch 14 is 576. More resolution reads smaller text and costs quadratically more tokens.
Design: why does your VLM hallucinate, and how do you measure and reduce it?
Causes: the language prior is strong (objects that usually co-occur get mentioned), the encoder lost the detail (resolution, too few tokens), and instruction data rewarded long confident descriptions. Measure with a POPE-style probe (balanced yes/no questions about present and absent objects, with random, popular and co-occurring absent objects; report the false-yes rate), a caption metric such as CHAIR (Rohrbach et al. 2018), and a text-only baseline. Reduce with higher resolution or tiling, better or unfrozen encoders, grounded and negative examples in instruction data (questions whose answer is "no"), preference tuning against hallucinated answers, and decoding that refuses to guess. Re-measure on held-out images, with error bars.
Design: a text-to-image system that returns an image in under 1 second.
Budget the passes: time one denoiser pass at the target resolution on the target GPU and multiply. 50 steps with guidance is 100 passes, so unless a pass takes under 10 ms it cannot meet 1 s, before the text encoder and decoder. Use a model distilled to 1 to 4 steps with guidance folded in (adversarial or consistency distillation), bf16 or fp8 weights, a compiled graph, the text encoder output cached for repeated prompts, and a fast decoder (or a tiny distilled decoder for previews). Generate at 512 to 768 and upscale if needed; batch requests per GPU; keep a few-step preview then refine path for quality. Measure the latency distribution, and check quality against the slow model with preference tests, because distillation loses variety.
Why can FID disagree with people?
It measures distance between Gaussian fits of Inception-v3 features, an ImageNet classifier's view: it is sensitive to ImageNet class statistics, resizing and compression, biased by sample count, and blind to prompt following and text rendering. For text-to-image work, report it next to prompt-alignment checks, CLIP-feature distances such as CMMD, and human preference.
CLIP's loss against SigLIP's: what changes?
CLIP applies a softmax over all captions in the batch for each image (and vice versa), so every pair's loss depends on the whole N × N similarity matrix. SigLIP scores each pair independently with a sigmoid (match or not, with a learned bias), so no global normalisation is needed: cheaper to shard across devices, better at small batches, and able to grow the batch further.
A multimodal LLM should also generate images: autoregressive tokens or diffusion?
Discrete tokens reuse the language-model stack, loss and serving (Chameleon, and, per its system card, GPT-4o image generation), but cost one pass per token and lose detail in the tokenizer. Diffusion or flow on continuous latents gives better images per FLOP and runs in tens of passes, but needs a second objective and sampler (Transfusion puts both in one transformer; others attach a separate diffusion decoder). Choose by what you must share (one context, editing in conversation), the latency budget and the quality bar.
