Latent lab. Why image generators work on a small code instead of pixels, built up from zero on the topic's running example: a plain autoencoder, a variational autoencoder (VAE), a VQ-VAE that turns an image into tokens, and then the real thing, the Stable Diffusion 1.5 autoencoder and its scaling factor 0.18215. Every tiny model here was trained for this page on Fashion-MNIST, and every picture and number is a recorded output, measured on Apple M1 Pro unless labelled published or derived.

Why a latentOne image, five modelsWhy an autoencoder cannot generateThe VAEInterpolationBeta and blurVQ-VAE and tokensThe SD autoencoderThe scaling factorMistakes and interviews

1. Why generate in a latent space

The problem. A 512 × 512 colour image is 786,432 numbers, and most of them encode detail the eye barely notices: the grain of a wall, the exact edge of a hair. A diffusion model runs its network 25 to 50 times for one image (the Diffusion lab measures this), so every step pays for every pixel. The LDM paper showed this with a rate-distortion plot of a pixel-space diffusion model: most of the bits go into imperceptible detail, the composition costs few (LDM paper page).

The idea. Train an autoencoder once: an encoder network squeezes the image into a small latent (also called the code; the narrow point is the bottleneck), a decoder network rebuilds the image from it, and training minimises the reconstruction loss, the difference between input and output. Then generate latents instead of pixels and decode once at the end. Stable Diffusion 1.5 keeps 64 × 64 × 4 = 16,384 numbers per 512 × 512 image, 48 times fewer derived from the VAE config.

The cost. A second network to train, and a ceiling: the generator can never produce detail the decoder cannot draw. Section 8 measures that ceiling for the SD decoder.

Here. The running example is Fashion-MNIST (grey 28 × 28 clothing, padded to 32 × 32 = 1,024 pixels; Reading tab and the root's src/data/README.md describe it). Every tiny model below shares one encoder and one decoder from the topic's code (src/data/nets.py, ConvAE: two stride-2 convolutions take 32 × 32 to 64 channels at 8 × 8; two transposed convolutions take it back). They differ only in what sits in the middle: 2 or 16 plain numbers (autoencoder), a mean and a spread per number (VAE), or 64 integers picked from a codebook (VQ-VAE). Same data order, same seed, steps at batch 128 each (about s each on the laptop's GPU).

2. One image through each model

Pick an image and a model and watch it go through: input, encoder, the code in the bottleneck, decoder, output beside the input. Switch the model and the same image goes through the other one, drawn at the same scale, so you see what each kind of bottleneck keeps.

The 16 fixed test images of the topic (the first test image of each class, then the second of classes 0 to 5). Outputs are the trained models' real reconstructions; the encoder and decoder panels show sizes, not activations. In the SD view the latent's four channels are the real 64 × 64 maps of the cat photo (each stretched to its own black-to-white range).

Predict: which keeps more of the image, a code of 16 plain numbers or 64 tokens from a codebook of 128 entries?
Measured on the 10,000 test images: the 16-number autoencoder reaches dB PSNR, the VQ-VAE with 64 tokens dB (and the 2-number autoencoder dB). A real number in a network is not infinitely precise in practice: the decoder can only use the precision training made it sensitive to, so spatial layout (64 positions, each with its own code) beats a few global numbers. That is one reason image tokenizers keep a grid. measured

3. Why a plain autoencoder does not generate

The problem. To generate, you pick a code and decode it. But which codes are valid? A plain autoencoder never says. Training only ever decodes the codes of real images, so the code space is a scattered cloud, with gaps between the clusters and at a scale nobody chose. A random code lands in a gap, or in the wrong place entirely.

Below, the left panel is the 2-number autoencoder, the right panel the 2-number VAE (section 4). Each dot is the code of one of 600 test images (the first 60 of each class). Drag or click in a panel to decode that point (it snaps to the nearest of 81 decodes precomputed on a 9 × 9 grid, the grey dots; arrow keys move it). The dashed circle is radius 2 around the origin, where 86% of draws from a standard Gaussian N(0, I) land (in 2-D, P(r < 2) = 1 − e−2) derived. Switch to decodes to see the whole grid of decoded images at once.

Autoencoder, 2 numbers

Box: z1 from to , z2 from to (where training happened to put the codes).

VAE, 2 numbers

Box: −3 to 3 on both axes, the scale the KL term asks for.

What the panels show: the autoencoder's codes spread over a box about 49 by 70 units wide, and the N(0, I) circle is a speck near the origin, smaller than one cell of the decode grid; the random-code samples below show what lives there (mostly bags and pullovers). The VAE's codes (here the means μ) fill a disc of radius about 3 around the origin, the scale of N(0, I), because the KL term pulls them there; the gaps between classes are small, so almost any point decodes to some garment.

Predict: decode 1,000 random codes from N(0, I) with the 16-number autoencoder. What comes out?
The topic's Fashion-MNIST classifier calls of them a Bag. The autoencoder's codes have a standard deviation between and per dimension, so N(0, I) samples all sit in one small region near the origin, and the decoder maps that whole region to one blob. A scale mismatch produces mode collapse without any training failure. measured

Measured: samples from random codes. 1,000 codes from each recipe, decoded, then scored by the topic's Fashion-MNIST classifier: the Fréchet distance (FD) between the samples' and the 10,000 test images' features in the classifier's 128-d feature space (the FID formula with a domain-specific network; lower is better), and the classifier's mean top-class probability. The floor is 1,000 real validation images scored the same way: FD (FD is biased upward at small sample sizes, so compare with this floor, not with 0). The first 8 samples of each recipe:

FD to the test set, 1,000 samples each (lower is better)

The same 1,000 Gaussian draws feed every 2-d model, and another fixed 1,000 every 16-d model. "Fitted Gaussian": mean and covariance of the codes of 10,000 training images, then z = mean + Lε with L its Cholesky factor. Scorer: fid.fd_fmnist in the root's src/data/. measured on Apple M1 Pro (CPU)

Three readings. N(0, I) fails for the autoencoder (FD at 16 numbers, against for the VAE), as expected. But a Gaussian fitted to the autoencoder's own codes does better than the VAE here (FD ): what makes a latent space usable is knowing where the codes are, and you can learn that after training. Ghosh et al. made this point with deterministic "regularised autoencoders" plus a density fitted afterwards (From Variational to Deterministic Autoencoders, 2019) published. What the VAE buys is that the density is N(0, I) by construction, with no second stage, and a space with no large holes. All of these tiny generators are far from the floor: a one-shot decoder from a simple Gaussian cannot model the data's many modes; this is why modern systems put a diffusion or autoregressive model on top of the latent instead of sampling it directly.

4. The VAE: an encoder that outputs a distribution

How it works. The VAE's encoder outputs, for each latent dimension, a mean μ and a log-variance log σ2: a little Gaussian per image instead of a point. Training decodes a random draw from it, and adds a penalty that pulls every image's Gaussian towards N(0, I):

z = μ(x) + σ(x) · ε,   ε ~ N(0, I)     loss = reconstruction(x, decoder(z)) + β · ½ Σj (μj2 + σj2 − 1 − log σj2)
ε
the randomness, drawn outside the network: the reparameterisation trick. Sampling z directly would block gradients; writing it as μ + σε makes z a differentiable function of μ and σ
KL
the second term is KL(N(μ, σ2) ‖ N(0, I)) in closed form, in nats: zero only when μ = 0 and σ = 1 (the code carries nothing)
β
1 gives the negative ELBO, the standard VAE loss; the derivation is on Variational inference and generative-model maths (sections 7 to 10). Section 6 below varies it

The code that trained every VAE on this page (the topic's shared code; src/data/nets.py lines 249 to 252 and objectives.py lines 130 to 136):

def forward(self, x): # ConvVAE mu, logvar = self.encode(x) z = mu + torch.exp(0.5 * logvar) * torch.randn_like(mu) # the reparameterisation trick return self.decode(z), mu, logvar def vae_loss(model, x, y=None, beta=1.0): """Negative ELBO (beta = 1) per image: reconstruction + beta * KL(q(z|x) || N(0, I)).""" logits, mu, logvar = model(x) rec = recon_bce(logits, x) kl = 0.5 * (mu.pow(2) + logvar.exp() - 1 - logvar).flatten(1).sum(1).mean() loss = rec + beta * kl return loss, {"loss": loss.item(), "rec": rec.item(), "kl": kl.item()}
last log line of the 16-number VAE, beta 1 (src/latent/runs/vae16_b1p0.jsonl): {"step": 5000, "sec": 114.99, "grad_norm": 89.1906, "loss": 239.70682, "rec": 222.66508, "kl": 17.04174}

Diffusers does the same in DiagonalGaussianDistribution.sample, x = self.mean + self.std * sample (models/autoencoders/vae.py line 711, v0.41.0); the SD encoder's output is split into mean and log-variance and the log-variance clamped to [−30, 20] (line 694).

The cost, measured. On the 10,000 test images the 16-number VAE pays nats of KL per image, and its reconstruction is worse than the plain autoencoder's: against nats, against dB PSNR. In return its codes sit where N(0, I) expects them. In the 2-number VAE the encoder's σ averages : each image claims a tiny ellipse of a space whose overall spread is 1 (click a point in the right-hand explorer above to see its ellipse).

When it matters, how to check. Watch the KL per dimension: a dimension whose KL is near 0 is unused (its μ is always about 0 and σ about 1); "active units" counts dimensions whose μ varies across images by more than 0.01 (Burda et al. 2015). The 16-number VAE at beta 1 uses of 16. When nearly all go inactive the decoder is ignoring the code: posterior collapse, common with strong decoders such as autoregressive ones (the Math page derives it).

5. Interpolation: walking between two images

A good latent space lets you walk from one image to another through plausible images. Below, the same two test images joined three ways: mixing pixels, and decoding points on the straight line between their codes in the 16-number autoencoder and in the 16-number VAE.

Pixels
Autoencoder latent (16 numbers)
VAE latent (16 numbers, beta 1, means)

t = 0, 1/8, ..., 1. The end points of the latent rows are reconstructions, not the originals, which is why they are softer than the pixel row's ends. measured

Pixel mixing gives a ghost of both garments at every step. Both latent paths give single garments that change shape. The VAE's middle frames tend to be the cleaner (its decoder was trained on noisy codes, so the space between two images is familiar ground), while the autoencoder's can turn blotchy; at this scale the difference is small, and the VAE's clear advantage is off the data, in the random-code test of section 3. In large latent diffusion models the same idea is used through the noise: interpolate the starting noise (spherically, since Gaussian noise lives near a sphere) rather than the clean latent (DDIM, section 5.3 and Appendix D.5).

6. Beta: the blur trade-off

The problem. The KL term is a price per bit the code carries about the image. Raise its weight β and the encoder sends less: reconstructions blur, dimensions switch off, but the codes hug N(0, I) more tightly, so random codes decode to more typical images. Lower it and you approach the plain autoencoder. Five 16-number VAEs, identical except for β, trained for this page:

Test images
Reconstructions at this β
Decoded from random codes z ~ N(0, I) (the same 8 draws at every β)

Left: each β is one point on a rate-distortion curve (bits about the image against reconstruction error, both in nats per image on the 10,000 test images). Right: the KL of each latent dimension at the chosen β. measured on Apple M1 Pro

Reading the sweep. From β 0.1 to 10 the KL falls from to nats per image and reconstruction error rises from to nats ( to dB): the blur you see. At β 10 only of 16 dimensions stay active; the rest are switched off because each bit costs too much. Random-code samples are best in the middle (FD at 0.3 and at 1) and worse at both ends: at 0.1 the codes drift from N(0, I) (FD ), at 10 the samples are confident but blurry and less varied (FD , class entropy nats against at 1). Higgins et al.'s β-VAE uses β > 1 on purpose, to trade reconstruction for disentangled factors (beta-VAE, ICLR 2017). measured

Why VAEs blur at all. Even at small β, a VAE trained with a per-pixel loss (here Bernoulli, often squared error) is rewarded for predicting the average of the images consistent with its code; an average of slightly different edges is a soft edge. The fixes are not in β: they are a loss that does not reward averaging (perceptual and adversarial losses, section 8) or a stronger generator on top of the latent (diffusion).

7. VQ-VAE: an image as tokens

How it works. Keep the latent as a grid (here 8 × 8 positions of 8 numbers), and replace each position's vector by the nearest of K learned vectors, the codebook (here K = 128). The image becomes 64 integers, image tokens, which a transformer can model exactly like words. The VQ-VAE (van den Oord et al. 2017) started the family of image tokenizers behind autoregressive image generators such as Parti and Chameleon. Nearest-neighbour lookup has no gradient, so the decoder's gradient is copied straight to the encoder (the straight-through estimator), and two extra terms train the codebook and keep the encoder near it:

loss = reconstruction + ‖sg[ze] − e‖2 + β ‖ze − sg[e]‖2
ze, e
the encoder's vector at one position and its nearest codebook vector
sg
stop-gradient: the first term moves only the codebook (the codebook loss), the second only the encoder (the commitment loss, β = 0.25 in the paper and here)
def quantize(self, ze): # src/latent/vq.py B, D, H, W = ze.shape flat = ze.permute(0, 2, 3, 1).reshape(-1, D) E = self.codebook.weight d = flat.pow(2).sum(1, keepdim=True) - 2 * flat @ E.t() + E.pow(2).sum(1)[None] idx = d.argmin(1) zq = E[idx].view(B, H, W, D).permute(0, 3, 1, 2) return zq, idx.view(B, H, W) def forward(self, x): ze = self.ae.encode(x) zq, idx = self.quantize(ze) z_st = ze + (zq - ze).detach() # straight-through estimator return self.ae.decode(z_st), ze, zq, idx

Read the library version critically: diffusers' VectorQuantizer keeps a known bug for backward compatibility, "due to a bug the beta term was applied to the wrong term" (models/autoencoders/vae.py lines 574 to 576 and 651 to 654, v0.41.0): with the default legacy=True, β multiplies the codebook term and the commitment term gets weight 1.

Codebook collapse. Codes that no encoder output is nearest to get no codebook-loss gradient, so they never move and are never used again: the effective vocabulary shrinks. The usual fixes: initialise the codebook from encoder outputs, update it by moving averages, use low-dimensional or normalised codes, or restart dead codes. Two VQ-VAEs trained here, the same in everything except that one replaces codes unused for 100 steps by random encoder outputs from the current batch (a restart, as in Jukebox, section 3.1, "Random restarts for embeddings"):

Codebook usage on the 10,000 test images (both runs; the selected one solid)
Codes used in each window of 100 training steps
The same image as tokens: pick an image, then point at a token to highlight every position with the same code

What the two runs show. Both start with all codes in use, and in both usage crashes within the first few hundred steps, as the encoder's outputs grow far beyond the tiny initial codebook (initialised uniformly in ±1/K, diffusers' default) and only the few codes nearest to them get pulled along: of 128 codes used in the window ending at step 200 in the plain run. With restarts the dead codes are re-seeded from encoder outputs and the codebook is full again by step ; without them recovery is slow, and after 5,000 steps of 128 codes are used on the test set (perplexity , against and with restarts). Reconstruction ended the same ( against dB). That matches Jukebox's own observation: "Models trained without random restarts can converge to the same test error and codebook usage but require more training steps" published. On a small codebook and an easy dataset the collapse heals; on large codebooks (thousands of codes) dead codes are the norm without a fix. measured

Tokens against numbers. 64 tokens of 7 bits are 448 bits, yet the VQ-VAE reconstructs better than the 16-number autoencoder ( against dB): a grid of local codes suits images. The token map shows how the codes are used: a test image takes 28 to 43 distinct codes for its 64 positions, and the same blank corner gets the same few codes across images (117, 72, 26 recur), while positions on the garment get codes of their own. Point at a token to see where else it appears.

Real tokenizers are much larger published: Chameleon's tokenizer "encodes a 512x512 image into 1024 discrete tokens from a codebook of size 8192" (arXiv 2405.09818); VQGAN added the perceptual and adversarial losses of section 8 to make tokens sharp (Esser et al. 2020). The native multimodal models that generate images token by token are compared on the Reading tab and the Model map.

8. The Stable Diffusion autoencoder

What it is. The autoencoder of Stable Diffusion 1.5 (AutoencoderKL in diffusers, 83,653,863 parameters, counted from the loaded module) maps 512 × 512 × 3 to 64 × 64 × 4: a downsampling factor f = 8 and 4 channels (latent_channels 4 and block_out_channels [128, 256, 512, 512] in the pinned vae/config.json) published config. It is called a VAE, but barely: its KL weight in the original training config is 0.000001 (latent-diffusion configs/autoencoder/autoencoder_kl_32x32x4.yaml line 11), a million times less than the beta 1 of section 4, so its codes are not pulled to N(0, I). What makes it sharp is the rest of the loss.

Its loss, LPIPSWithDiscriminator (ldm/modules/losses/contperceptual.py lines 48 to 83): an L1 pixel loss plus a perceptual loss, LPIPS, the distance between the two images' features inside a pretrained network (Zhang et al. 2018), plus a tiny KL, plus, from step 50,001 (disc_start), an adversarial loss from a patch discriminator, a small network trained to tell real image patches from reconstructed ones, weighted adaptively so its gradient matches the reconstruction gradient's size (calculate_adaptive_weight, lines 32 to 42). Pixel losses reward the average of the plausible images, which is blurry; the perceptual and adversarial terms reward texture that looks right even when it is not pixel-exact. The recipe is VQGAN's (Esser et al. 2020) with a KL in place of the codebook (LDM paper page, Stage 1).

Measured: the 16 test images through it. Encode (posterior mean), decode, compare with the original. Float32 weights; float16 for comparison.

PSNR in dB and SSIM on the 512 × 512 RGB image; latent std over the 4 × 64 × 64 raw latent; posterior σ: the mean of the encoder's own standard deviation. measured on Apple M1 Pro (MPS), diffusers 0.41.0, SD 1.5 at revision 451f4fe16113.

Same pixel error, different picture. For three images, the reconstruction beside a Gaussian blur of the original whose strength was searched until its PSNR equals the reconstruction's. If PSNR were the whole story the two would look equally good:

Crops of 160 × 160 pixels of the 512 × 512 images (small WebP thumbnails, so compression adds a little softness to all three). Feature distance: cosine distance between the 2,048-d Inception pool features (torch-fidelity's inception-v3-compat) of the original and the image, a stand-in for LPIPS, which is not installed here; lower is closer. src/latent/perc_demo.py. measured (CPU)

What the measurements say. The decoder is good but not lossless: photographs come back at 26.7 to 30.9 dB, the synthetic graphics (shapes, text, chart, clock) at 32.3 to 37.5 dB, and the busiest generated image (the puppy on grass) at dB. That ceiling binds every SD 1.5 image: fine grass, small faces and small text are redrawn by the decoder, never copied. Float16 changes PSNR by at most 0.1 dB here and produces no NaNs. The posterior's own σ is about 0.00005 to 0.001 against a latent std of 4 to 7: with a KL weight of 10−6 the "variational" part is negligible, and the encoder is in practice deterministic.

The same-PSNR comparison splits by image. On the cat and the Hubble field (and the stop sign, not shown), the reconstruction is far closer in deep features than the equally-scored blur (cat against ; Hubble against ): the blur erases faint galaxies and fur the decoder redraws. SSIM does not agree everywhere (on the Hubble field it prefers the blur, against ), a reminder that SSIM is also a local pixel statistic. On the text card the matching blur is only px and wins on every measure: on flat graphics the decoder's errors are not blur but small artefacts along edges, which is why SD-class models garble small text. measured

9. The scaling factor 0.18215

The problem. A diffusion model adds noise of standard deviation about 1 to its input, on a fixed schedule. The schedule assumes the input itself has a scale near 1; the SD autoencoder's raw latents do not, because its tiny KL weight never asked for it. The LDM authors divide the latent by its standard deviation measured on the first training batch (scale_by_std, ldm/models/diffusion/ddpm.py line 489: 1. / z.flatten().std()), and SD 1.x froze the result as scale_factor: 0.18215. Without it, the LDM paper says, the SNR is "very high" and the model "allocates a lot of semantic detail early on" (LDM paper page, D.1).

Where it lives in code. The pinned SD 1.5 vae/config.json has no scaling_factor key; diffusers falls back to the class default (scaling_factor: float = 0.18215, autoencoder_kl.py line 90, v0.41.0). Pipelines multiply after encoding (img2img line 771) and divide before decoding (text-to-image line 1085). Other autoencoders have other factors: SDXL's 0.13025, and 16-channel ones with a shift as well (the Model map lists them).

Measured on the 16 test images: raw latent std , so 1 / std = ; after × 0.18215 the std is . measured

Before and after: the same latent noised at the same timestep with the same noise, once in scaled units (what the U-Net was trained on) and once raw (factor forgotten), each decoded. The raw one stays recognisable far longer, so at a given t the model is shown a far cleaner input than it was trained to expect:

Three ways to get it wrong, measured in a real pipeline.

Decoding the cat's encoded latent with the factor applied wrongly (VAE only)
Image-to-image on the cat (prompt "a photograph of a tabby cat", strength 0.6, 25 DPM-Solver steps, guidance 7.5, seed 0) with the VAE's factor set to each value
Text-to-image ("", seed 1, 25 steps): the same final latent decoded three ways

SD 1.5 fp16 with attention slicing, src/latent/sd_scale.py. Pixel std: the standard deviation of the 0 to 255 pixel values averaged over R, G, B (contrast). measured on Apple M1 Pro (MPS)

Reading the results. Over all 16 images the raw latent's std is , and one over it is : the LDM authors' recipe, rerun on 16 images, lands within 0.3% of 0.18215. Forgetting the factor makes the latent 1 / 0.18215 = 5.49 times too large, so its SNR is 30 times higher at every timestep derived; in the noising strip the raw cat is still recognisable at t = 999 ( dB) while the correctly scaled one is mostly noise by t = 300 ( dB). At the decoder, forgetting to divide shrinks the latent and gives a flat, grey ghost (pixel std against in red), dividing twice blows colours out ().

In the pipeline runs, the wrong factor changes the result without any error message. Image-to-image with SDXL's smaller factor 0.13025 feeds the U-Net a latent 1.4 times too small and comes back over-contrasted (pixel std against in red with the right factor); with no factor at all the latent is 5.5 times too large, the denoiser removes "noise" that is really image, and the result is a smeared, low-contrast cat (). At the end of text-to-image, forgetting to divide gives a grey fog of the right picture ( against ), and SDXL's factor over-saturates it (). The final latent of that run, in the U-Net's scaled units, has std . measured

10. Common mistakes, checks and interview questions

Sampling a plain autoencoder from N(0, I)
Its codes live at whatever scale training chose (standard deviation 5 to 9.5 per dimension here), so N(0, I) samples sit in one corner and decode to one blob (section 3). Check: print the mean and std of the codes of real images before sampling; fit a density to them, or use a VAE.
Reading a lower reconstruction loss as a better generator
The plain autoencoder reconstructs best and generates worst from N(0, I). Reconstruction and generation are different measurements; score samples separately (FD with a stated sample size and floor).
Turning beta up to "fix" blurry samples
Higher beta makes reconstructions blurrier and switches dimensions off (section 6). Blur comes from the pixel loss; the cure is a perceptual or adversarial loss, or a stronger generator on top of the latent.
Ignoring codebook usage in a VQ model
A codebook of 128 with a fraction in use is a smaller codebook that cost the full size. Log codes used and perplexity during training (section 7); restart dead codes or initialise from encoder outputs.
Trusting a library's commitment loss without reading it
diffusers' VectorQuantizer applies β to the wrong term unless legacy=False (vae.py lines 574 to 576). Read the loss you train with.
Using the wrong scaling factor, or none
Each autoencoder has its own (SD 1.x 0.18215, SDXL 0.13025, some with a shift too). Missing at encode time, the U-Net sees inputs far cleaner than the timestep says (section 9); missing at decode time, colours wash out or blow up. Check: the std of scaled latents of real images should be near 1, and a round trip encode, scale, unscale, decode must reproduce the image.
Measuring an autoencoder only by PSNR
A blur with the same PSNR as the SD reconstruction looks far worse (section 8). Report a perceptual measure (LPIPS, or at least SSIM) and look at crops at full resolution, including text.
Running a VAE decoder in float16 without checking
SD 1.5's decoder is fine in float16 here (table in section 8), but some autoencoders overflow in half precision (the SDXL VAE is the known case, which is why a separate fp16-fixed SDXL VAE exists). Check for NaNs and compare with float32 once.

Interview questions

Why do latent diffusion models not diffuse in pixel space?
Cost and focus: a 512 × 512 image has 786,432 numbers against 16,384 in SD's latent (48 times fewer), and the denoiser runs 25 to 50 times per image; the autoencoder removes imperceptible detail once, so the generator spends its capacity on composition. The price is the decoder's ceiling and a second model to train.
What does the reparameterisation trick do, and why is it needed?
It writes the sample as z = μ + σε with ε drawn outside the network, so z is a differentiable function of the encoder's outputs and backpropagation reaches μ and σ. Sampling z directly from N(μ, σ2) has no gradient path.
Why are VAE samples blurry, and what fixes it?
A per-pixel loss is minimised by the average of the images consistent with the code, and averages are soft; the KL term adds noise to the code, which widens that set. Fixes: perceptual and adversarial losses (as in the SD autoencoder and VQGAN), or a powerful prior over the latent (diffusion, autoregressive).
What is codebook collapse and how do you prevent it?
Codes that are never nearest to any encoder output receive no gradient and stay unused, shrinking the vocabulary. Prevent with data-dependent initialisation, EMA codebook updates, dead-code restarts, or low-dimensional normalised codes; monitor codes used and perplexity.
What is the 0.18215 in Stable Diffusion, and what breaks without it?
One over the standard deviation of SD's raw latents, measured by the LDM authors on a training batch, so latents enter the diffusion process at unit scale. Without it the latents are about 5.5 times too large: at every timestep the signal-to-noise ratio is about 30 times higher than the schedule assumes, and decoding without dividing gives washed-out images.
Design: you need a tokenizer for an autoregressive image model. What do you choose and measure?
A VQ (or lookup-free) tokenizer with a 2-D grid of tokens; pick the downsampling factor (tokens per image sets sequence length and cost) and codebook size (bits per token), train with perceptual and adversarial losses, and measure reconstruction (PSNR, LPIPS, rFID), codebook usage and perplexity, and how well a small prior models the tokens. Trade-off: fewer tokens are cheaper to generate but reconstruct worse.
A colleague's img2img outputs come back smeared and low-contrast, or over-contrasted, with no error. First check?
The VAE scaling factor: encoded latents not multiplied by the model's factor (smeared, section 9) or multiplied by another model's (over-contrasted). Print the std of the latents fed to the U-Net; it should be near 1.

What transfers from this laptop

Measured on Apple M1 Pro: every tiny model trained for steps in about 100 to 120 s on MPS (float32, batch 128, about 1.1 GB peak). The shapes of the results transfer: the scale mismatch that sinks N(0, I) sampling for a plain autoencoder, the rate-distortion trade-off of β, codebook collapse without restarts, the blur of pixel losses, and every scaling-factor effect (pure arithmetic on the same weights). The absolute numbers do not: FD here uses a small Fashion-MNIST classifier and 1,000 samples, so it is comparable only within this page, and longer training or bigger models would move every model's numbers. Timings on a datacenter GPU would be far shorter.

Latent lab. Code and recorded outputs: src/latent/ in the page folder (train_lt.py, vq.py, eval_lt.py, sd_vae.py, sd_scale.py, perc_demo.py, make_data.py; runs in runs/, numbers in out/). Built 17 October 2026.

A diffusion model generates by learning to undo noise. This lab builds one from zero on the running example (Fashion-MNIST: 28 × 28 grey clothing in 10 classes), trains it on the M1 Pro's GPU for minutes, samples it every common way, and then runs the same experiments on Stable Diffusion v1.5. Every image and number below comes from code in src/diff/ and its recorded output, measured on Apple M1 Pro (MPS) on , unless labelled published or derived.

1. Forward process2. Schedules3. Denoiser4. Sampling5. Steps vs quality6. Guidance7. Stable Diffusion8. Debugging9. InterviewSources

How to read the scores: FD is the Fréchet distance between 1,000 samples and the 10,000 test images in the feature space of a small Fashion-MNIST classifier (lower is better; 1,000 real validation images score , the floor at this sample size); accuracy is how often that classifier recognises the class the sample was asked for; diversity is the mean distance between samples of the same class in that feature space (real images: ). Scores are comparable within this lab and the Flow lab only (shared code in src/data/fid.py; why not Inception FID at this size: the root's Reading tab, section 9).

1. The forward process: destroying an image on purpose

The problem. We want to draw new images from the distribution the training images came from, but nobody can write that distribution down. Going the other way is easy: take a real image and add noise until nothing is left. Diffusion learns to reverse that destruction one small step at a time; then it can start from pure noise, which anyone can sample, and walk back to an image.

How it works. At each of T = 1,000 steps the forward process shrinks the image a little and adds a little Gaussian noise: step t adds noise of variance βt, the noise schedule. Because Gaussians add up to a Gaussian, you never have to simulate the steps one by one: the noisy image at any step has a closed form.

xt = √āt · x0 + √(1 − āt) · ε,   ε ~ N(0, I)
x0
the clean image, pixels scaled to [−1, 1]
αt
1 − βt, the fraction of variance a step keeps
āt
α1 α2 … αt ("alpha bar"): how much of the original signal's variance survives to step t; it falls from about 1 to about 0
ε
one draw of standard Gaussian noise, the same size as the image

This one line is all of training's data pipeline: pick an image, a random t and random noise, and the noisy input is ready (diffusers does exactly this in scheduling_ddpm.py line 608, v0.41.0). The derivation of the closed form is on the math page, section 12.

The same ten images and the same noise, two schedules, one timestep

Images: the first Fashion-MNIST test image of each class. The noise is drawn in your browser from a fixed seed (the same ε for every t and both rows), so the only thing that changes between the rows is āt. Schedule formulas as in diffusers v0.41.0 (linear, squaredcos_cap_v2, scaled_linear, lines 214 to 229).

Predict, then reveal. Under DDPM's linear schedule, at t = 500 (half way), how much of the image's amplitude is left?
About a quarter: √ā500 = under the linear schedule, against under the cosine one derived. Move the slider to 500 and look: the linear row is mostly noise at half way, which is the cosine schedule's whole motivation (next section).

2. Noise schedules and the signal-to-noise ratio

The problem. Schedules are written as lists of β, which are hard to compare. What matters to the model is how much signal is left against how much noise at each step: the signal-to-noise ratio, SNR(t) = āt / (1 − āt). On a log scale it falls from large (almost clean) to tiny (almost pure noise), and two schedules are best compared by where along t they spend their steps.

log10 SNR against timestep, three schedules

  • Linear (DDPM, β from 10−4 to 0.02): SNR drops below 1 at t = , so about of the training timesteps are noise-dominated derived. On small images that tail carries little information; Nichol and Dhariwal (2021) proposed the cosine schedule so that āt falls slowly at both ends (SNR = 1 at t = ).
  • Scaled-linear (Stable Diffusion 1.5, β from 0.00085 to 0.012, linear in √β): at the last step √ā is still , so of the latent's amplitude survives the "full" noising. Training never shows the model pure noise, but sampling starts from it: Lin et al. (2023) traced washed-out images (the model cannot make very dark or very bright pictures) to this and proposed rescaling to zero terminal SNR. diffusers cites that paper beside its timestep-spacing options (DDIM line 357), which matter in section 7.
  • Resolution shifts the schedule. The same SNR destroys a large image less than a small one, because neighbouring pixels average the noise away; Hoogeboom, Heek and Salimans (2023) shift the schedule with image size, and Stable Diffusion 3 shifts its timesteps for the same reason (Esser et al. 2024). A schedule tuned at 32 × 32 is not automatically right at 1024 × 1024.

The tiny model here uses the linear schedule, DDPM's own, so that the lab reproduces the classic setup; the shared code also has the cosine one (objectives.betas_cosine).

3. The denoiser, and what it is trained to predict

The network. The denoiser takes the noisy image xt, the timestep t and (here) the class label, and returns a tensor of the image's shape. Ours is the shared TinyUNet: parameters, a U-Net (a convolutional network that shrinks the image from 32 to 16 to 8 pixels and grows it back, with skip connections between matching sizes and self-attention at 8 × 8). The timestep enters as a sinusoidal embedding and the label as a learned embedding with an 11th "no label" row, both added inside every residual block.

Three things it can be asked for. Given xt and t, the clean image and the noise determine each other, so a network can be trained to output any of these, and the sampler converts:

TargetDefinitionClean image from the outputUsed by
ε (noise)the noise that was addedx̂0 = (xt − √(1−ā) ε̂) / √āDDPM, Stable Diffusion 1.x
x0 (clean image)the image itselfthe outputsome cascades; flow models predict a close cousin
v (velocity)√ā ε − √(1−ā) x0x̂0 = √ā xt − √(1−ā) v̂Salimans and Ho 2022; Stable Diffusion 2 768-v

Look at the ε row at t = 999: √ā is , so any error in ε̂ is multiplied by on its way to x̂0. The v row has no division. That difference is invisible at 50 steps and decisive at 1 step (section 5). Why predicting noise is the right loss for DDPM, from the ELBO, is on the DDPM paper page and the math page, sections 13 and 15.

The training step, as it ran (src/diff/train_ddpm.py); the label is replaced by the null class 10% of the time so that one network also learns the unconditional model guidance needs (section 6):

def loss_fn(model, b):
    x0, y = b
    t = torch.randint(0, sched.T, (x0.shape[0],), device=dev)
    eps = torch.randn_like(x0)
    pred = model(sched.q_sample(x0, t, eps), t.float() / sched.T, drop_labels(y, 0.1))
    loss = F.mse_loss(pred, target(x0, eps, t))     # target: eps, or v = sqrt(abar) eps - sqrt(1 - abar) x0
    return loss, {"loss": loss.item()}

The runs. Two models with one recipe and one change, the target: batch 128, AdamW at 5 × 10−4 after 200 warm-up steps, gradient clipping at 1, an exponential moving average (EMA) of the weights with decay 0.999 used for all sampling, steps each ( minutes at steps per second, peak MPS driver memory , which counts cached blocks and the 2,048-image evaluation at the end). Checkpoints are kept for the Flow lab, which trains the same network with the same recipe and step count.

Where the error lives: validation error by timestep (EMA weights, 2,048 validation images)

What the chart shows. The noise is hardest to guess when there is almost none (small t: is that speck noise or a stitch?), and the clean image is hardest to guess when there is almost no image left (large t). The ε loss weights every timestep's noise error equally, which is the same as weighting the clean-image error by the SNR, so it spends its effort on nearly clean images; the v loss sits between the two. Same network, same data: the target only moves the emphasis, as the Reading tab says.

4. Sampling: walking back from noise

The problem. The trained network only answers "given this noisy image at step t, what was the noise?". A sampler turns that answer into a path from pure noise to an image: a rule for where to go next and how many steps to take. Every sampler below uses the same trained weights; only the rule changes.

  • DDPM, ancestral (Ho et al. 2020): estimate the clean image x̂0, move to the average of where xt could have come from given x̂0 (the posterior mean), then add fresh noise. Built for the 1,000 small steps it was trained on; the fresh noise means the same start gives a different image each run.
  • DDIM (Song, Meng and Ermon 2020): the same trained model, but no fresh noise: keep the predicted noise as the direction and jump straight to the previous noise level, xprev = √āprev x̂0 + √(1 − āprev) ε̂. Deterministic (same noise, same image) and valid for any number of steps, because it follows the probability-flow ODE that the math page, section 16 derives.
  • DPM-Solver++ and Euler (Lu et al. 2022; Karras et al. 2022): treat that ODE as an ODE and integrate it with better numerical methods. DPM-Solver++ (2M, the diffusers default, line 227) reuses the previous step's prediction to take second-order steps at no extra network cost; Euler is the first-order method in the noise-level parametrisation.

DDIM, written out (src/diff/samplers.py, the code that made the animation below). Run on the trained model for 10 steps from the same 16 noise images, it matches diffusers' DDIMScheduler (trailing spacing) to (largest absolute difference in any pixel, float32 on MPS):

def ddim(net, abar, x, y, n, s=1.0, pred="eps", trace=None):
    ts = trailing(n)                                   # e.g. n = 4: 999, 749, 499, 249
    for i, t in enumerate(ts):
        ab = abar[t]
        ab_prev = abar[ts[i + 1]] if i + 1 < n else torch.ones_like(ab)
        eps, x0 = to_eps_x0(guided(net, x, t, y, s), x, ab, pred)
        x = ab_prev.sqrt() * x0 + (1 - ab_prev).sqrt() * eps       # jump to the previous noise level
    return x

diffusers v0.41.0 does the same in scheduling_ddim.py lines 456 and 491; the DDPM step's posterior mean and variance are scheduling_ddpm.py lines 534 to 535 and 388, and the hand-written ddpm() beside ddim() follows them.

The same noise through 1, 4, 20 and 50 steps

Three classes (dress, sandal, bag), the same three noise images in every mode; DDIM unless marked DDPM; no guidance (s = 1). Recorded frames from sample_tiny.py, shown at 16 grey levels.

What to notice. Switch to the model's guess at 20 steps: over the first third of the steps x̂0 turns from amplified noise into a rough, noisy outline of the final garment, and the remaining steps clean it up and add edges and texture; the 20-step and 50-step results are almost the same image, because DDIM follows one deterministic path from a given noise. Coarse structure is decided at high noise, detail at low noise, which is why skipping steps late hurts less than skipping them early. (At the very first step this noise-predicting model's guess is still mostly amplified noise, for the reason section 3 gives; a v-model's first guess is the blurred average, section 5.) The DDPM mode starts from the same noise but ends somewhere else: its fresh noise at every step makes it a different sample.

5. Steps against quality against time

The cost. Every step is one network evaluation (two with guidance), so the step count is the price of an image. Here one evaluation of the tiny U-Net takes ms for one image and ms for a batch of 1,000 on the M1 Pro's GPU; 1,000 DDPM steps for 1,000 images took s, DDIM at 20 steps s.

Predict, then reveal. Same model, same noise, 10 steps each. Which scores better: DDPM's ancestral sampler or DDIM?
Here, DDPM: FD against for DDIM, class accuracy against measured. The textbook answer is DDIM: the DDIM paper reports its deterministic sampler far ahead at 10 to 100 steps on CIFAR-10, and that is why it exists. The difference is the model. Ours trained for minutes and its noise predictions are still wrong in ways that pile up along a deterministic path; DDPM's fresh noise at every step lets later steps correct earlier mistakes (Karras et al. 2022, section 4, make this argument and add a tuned amount of noise to their own sampler). DDIM stops improving at by 250 steps; DDPM keeps going to at 1,000. A sampler ranking measured on one model does not transfer to another.

1,000 samples per point, four samplers, the same trained model

Look at them: one sample per class, the same ten noise images everywhere

Euler is not offered here: its samples and scores match DDIM's (chart above). Shown at 16 grey levels; scores use the full 8-bit samples.

Noise or v at one step. The ε-model's single DDIM step divides its noise error by √ā999 (section 3); the v-model, trained identically, has nothing to divide. One step is a bad idea for both, but only one of them fails by blowing up:

6. Classifier-free guidance

The problem. A conditional model asked for "sandal" produces something sandal-like, but its samples drift: some are ambiguous, some look like another class. We want a knob that trades variety for adherence to the condition, without training a separate classifier (Ho and Salimans 2022).

How it works. Train one network both with and without the label (the 10% dropout in section 3). At sampling, evaluate it both ways and extrapolate from the unconditional prediction past the conditional one:

ε̂ = εu + s · (εc − εu)
εc, εu
the prediction with the label (or prompt) and with the null label (or empty prompt)
s
the guidance scale: 0 is the unconditional model, 1 the plain conditional model, above 1 pushes further in the direction the condition points

This is diffusers' convention, pipeline_stable_diffusion.py line 1055. Two traps: the pipeline only runs the unconditional branch when the scale is above 1 (line 764), so guidance_scale=0 there is the plain conditional model, not the unconditional one; and papers often write the same formula as εc + w (εc − εu), where w = s − 1 (the shared objectives.py does). The cost: two evaluations per step, run as one batch of two (line 1037). The derivation, and a toy showing the lost diversity, are on the math page, section 17.

Guidance on the tiny model: DDIM, 50 steps, the same noise at every scale

The same on Stable Diffusion v1.5: one prompt, one seed, 25 DPM-Solver++ steps

7. Stable Diffusion v1.5: steps and time on a real model

The same questions on the pinned SD v1.5 (fp16 on the M1 Pro's GPU, attention slicing on, 512 × 512, guidance 7.5, the prompt and seed of section 6). Its denoiser works on a 4 × 64 × 64 latent rather than pixels (the Latent lab covers the autoencoder), but the samplers are the same code paths as on the tiny model.

Steps, and where the sampler starts

The timestep-spacing trap. SD 1.5's scheduler config has steps_offset 1 and no timestep_spacing, so DDIM falls back to its default "leading" (scheduling_ddim.py lines 365 to 370): with n steps it uses timesteps 0, 1000/n, 2000/n, … plus 1, so its first step is never t = 999. With 1 step it asks the model to denoise pure noise as if it were step , an almost clean image, and the result is noise. "trailing" starts at 999 (lines 371 to 376), the fix Lin et al. (2023) recommend; DPM-Solver's default, "linspace", also starts at 999. In the gallery, DDIM with leading spacing at 4 steps (timesteps 751, 501, 251, 1) gives a pale, foggy scene with no lighthouse, while trailing spacing at 4 steps (999, 749, 499, 249) gives a dark but recognisable silhouette with its lighthouse: same model, same noise, same number of network calls. At 25 or 50 steps the difference is small; at 1 to 4 steps, the schedule your sampler walks matters as much as the model.

Where the seconds go: one 512 × 512 image, measured piece by piece

What transfers to a datacenter GPU. The counts transfer: steps × (2 with guidance) U-Net passes, one decode, and the denoiser dominating. The seconds do not: an M1 Pro's GPU in fp16 with attention slicing (chosen here to keep memory near 4.5 GB) is many times slower per pass than a datacenter GPU, and the ratio of a batch-2 pass to a batch-1 pass depends on how much spare compute the device has, which is why guidance costs here close to twice the time per step but can cost less on a large GPU at batch 1.

8. Debugging a diffusion model: symptom, cause, check

SymptomLikely causeHow to check
Pure noise or saturated blotches at every step countPrediction type in the sampler differs from training (a v-model sampled as ε)Compare prediction_type in the scheduler config with the training code. Here: FD , accuracy at 50 steps (section 5's last strip)
Fine at 50 steps, noise at 1 to 4Timestep spacing that never starts at the last step ("leading"); or an ε-model asked for one stepPrint scheduler.timesteps; the first entry should be the last training step (section 7)
More steps stop helpingThe deterministic sampler has converged; the model's own error is now the limit (DDIM here: FD at 50 steps, at 250)Try a stochastic sampler at many steps (DDPM 1,000: ), guidance, or more training; more ODE steps will not help
Oversaturated colours, harsh contrast, repeated motifsGuidance scale too highSweep the scale at a fixed seed; watch saturation and diversity (section 6)
Samples ignore the class or promptGuidance off (scale ≤ 1 in diffusers), or the null condition never seen in trainingCheck the label or prompt dropout rate in training and do_classifier_free_guidance at sampling
Washed out, never very dark or very brightNon-zero terminal SNR (SD 1.5's schedule leaves of the signal at the last step)Compute ā at the last training step; consider zero-terminal-SNR rescaling and v-prediction (Lin et al. 2023)
Loss falls but samples stay blobsToo few steps of training, or sampling from the raw weights instead of the EMASample from both; plot loss by timestep (section 3)
Loss looks flat and tinyThe ε loss is dominated by easy, high-noise timesteps (its error at t = 999 is )Log the loss in timestep buckets, not one average

9. Interview questions

Why can diffusion training sample any timestep without running the earlier ones?

Because the forward process is a chain of Gaussians, xt given x0 is Gaussian in closed form: xt = √āt x0 + √(1 − āt) ε. One line makes the training input for any t.

What is the difference between DDPM and DDIM sampling, and can you use DDIM on a DDPM-trained model?

Same training; DDIM drops the fresh noise and follows the deterministic probability-flow path, so it works with 10 to 50 steps and the same noise always gives the same image. Yes, no retraining: the samplers in section 5 all run on one checkpoint. Which wins depends on the model: on this under-trained one DDPM beat DDIM at every step count from 4 up, because its fresh noise corrects the model's errors.

ε, x0 or v: which would you predict, and why?

They are interchangeable given xt; what differs is the loss weighting across noise levels and the numerical behaviour at high noise. ε is the DDPM default and fine at many steps; v avoids dividing by √ā near pure noise, which matters for few-step sampling, distillation and zero-terminal-SNR schedules (section 5's one-step comparison).

What does classifier-free guidance cost, and what does it buy?

Two denoiser evaluations per step (usually one batch of two) and 10 to 20% of training steps with the condition dropped. It buys adherence to the condition and cleaner samples at the cost of diversity; too high a scale oversaturates. Here, on the tiny model, class accuracy rose from at s = 1 to at s = 3 while diversity fell from to .

Your 4-step samples are noise but 50-step samples are fine. What do you check first?

The timesteps the scheduler actually walks (scheduler.timesteps): with "leading" spacing the first step is far below the last training step. Then the prediction type and whether the model was trained for few steps at all.

How would you cut a text-to-image model's latency by 10 times?

Count network passes: steps × 2 with guidance. Use a better solver (50 to 20 to 25 steps), distil guidance into the model (one pass per step), then distil steps (consistency or adversarial distillation to 1 to 4), and only then shave the per-pass time (lower precision, compilation, a smaller denoiser or latent). The Reading tab, section 10 has the calculator.

A flow-matching model generates by moving points: it learns a velocity for every point and every moment, and an image is made by starting at random noise and following those velocities until you arrive at data. This lab builds the idea from zero on a 2-D toy you can run in the page, then trains the same tiny U-Net as the Diffusion lab with the flow-matching objective instead, with the same recipe and the same number of training steps, and compares the two at equal sampling steps. Every image and number comes from code in src/flow/ and its recorded output, measured on Apple M1 Pro on , unless labelled published or derived.

1. Transport2. Objective3. ODE solvers4. Flow vs diffusion5. Reflow6. One family7. Guidance8. Where used9. Debugging10. InterviewSources

Scores on images are the Diffusion lab's, computed by the same code so the two labs share one table: FD is the Fréchet distance between 1,000 samples (100 per class) and the 10,000 test images in the feature space of a small Fashion-MNIST classifier (lower is better; 1,000 real validation images score , the floor at this sample size); accuracy is how often that classifier recognises the requested class; diversity is the mean distance between same-class samples in that space (real images: ).

1. Generating as transport

The problem. As in diffusion, we can sample noise easily and want samples of data. Diffusion gets there by learning to undo a noising process step by step. Flow matching asks a more direct question: if every noise point had to travel to some data point over one unit of time, what velocity field (an arrow at every position x and time t saying which way and how fast to move) would carry the whole cloud of noise onto the cloud of data?

How it works. Write t = 0 for noise and t = 1 for data (the convention of Lipman et al. and of this topic's shared code). A sample is made by solving an ordinary differential equation (ODE): start at x(0) drawn from a standard Gaussian and move with dx/dt = vθ(x, t), where vθ is the network. Nothing is random after the start: the same noise always gives the same output, like DDIM. Such a model is a continuous normalizing flow; what was new in 2022 is the cheap way to train it (section 2).

The toy, live: 400 noise points flowing onto a ring of 8 Gaussians

Four tiny networks (3 inputs: x, y, t; three hidden layers of ; parameters each) trained by src/flow/toy2d.py on CPU in s, embedded as 8-bit weights and run by your browser. Dots are coloured by the mode they end on (grey: between modes); arrows show which way the sampler moves from each spot at the current time. Every model starts from the same noise.

Steps

What to try. Flow matching at 1 step: every point moves towards the middle of the ring, where there is no data. Press Before / after reflow: on the same noise, the reflowed model lands most points on a mode in one step. Then 64 steps: all four models arrive, and the trails show why few steps fail for some of them: their paths bend.

2. The objective: regress the straight-line velocity

The problem. The velocity field that carries noise onto data is unknown; we only have samples of both ends. Training a flow by simulating the ODE and comparing the outputs (the older way to train continuous normalizing flows) needs an ODE solve per training step. Flow matching avoids any simulation.

How it works. Draw a noise x0, a training image x1 and a time t uniform in [0, 1]. Put a point on the straight line between them and ask the network for the velocity of that line, which is the same at every t:

xt = (1 − t) x0 + t x1,   loss = ‖ vθ(xt, t) − (x1 − x0) ‖²
x0
Gaussian noise, the same shape as an image
x1
a training image (scaled to [−1, 1])
x1 − x0
the target: the constant velocity of the straight path from that noise to that image

That is the whole training loop: one network call and one mean squared error, exactly as cheap as a DDPM step. This is conditional flow matching (CFM) with straight paths, called rectified flow by Liu et al. and the conditional optimal-transport path by Lipman et al. (both 2022, published). The code the image model trained with, from the topic's shared src/data/objectives.py (lines ):



The same path in Meta's reference library (facebookresearch/flow_matching at commit 11568d3): CondOTScheduler sets αt = t, σt = 1 − t (flow_matching/path/scheduler/scheduler.py lines 108 to 113) and the affine path builds x_t = sigma_t * x_0 + alpha_t * x_1 and dx_t = d_sigma_t * x_0 + d_alpha_t * x_1 (flow_matching/path/affine.py lines 89 to 90), which is x1 − x0. In torchcfm (commit 7c65385) the same two lines are t * x1 + (1 - t) * x0 and x1 - x0 (torchcfm/conditional_flow_matching.py lines 83 and 154).


Why it works, and why the paths still bend. Many straight lines pass through the same point x at time t, from different noises to different images, and they disagree on the direction. A network trained with a squared error learns their average: the marginal velocity, which provably moves the whole noise distribution onto the data distribution (Lipman et al.'s theorem). But an average of crossing lines is a curved flow: each sample's path bends as it goes, because the set of lines it is "averaging over" changes with t. At t = 0 every line through a point is equally likely to go to any image, so the velocity points at the mean of the data: the middle of the ring, or, for images, a grey blur.


The pairs a model is trained on


60 noise points (blue) joined to the data points (red) they are paired with in training. Random pairs: what plain flow matching uses. OT pairs: the same samples re-paired inside the batch to minimise total squared distance (Tong et al. 2023's minibatch optimal transport). Reflow pairs: each noise joined to where the trained flow takes it.







Crossing lines are what bend the learned paths. The two fixes in this lab both remove crossings: pick better pairs while training (OT), or retrain on the pairs the flow itself produces, which never cross because an ODE's paths cannot cross (reflow, section 5).


Predict. A flow-matching model trained on Fashion-MNIST is sampled with a single Euler step: x1 = x0 + vθ(x0, 0). What comes out?



A blur. At t = 0 the best squared-error answer is the average direction to every image of that class, so one step lands on (roughly) the class mean. Measured on this lab's model: 1 Euler step scores FD  with class accuracy  and diversity  (real images ): blurry averages that the classifier recognises about half the time, with almost no variety. Strip in section 4.


Training the image model. The Diffusion lab's recipe, unchanged: the same TinyUNet ( parameters; time t in [0, 1] and the class label as inputs), batch 128, AdamW at 5e-4 with 200 warm-up steps, gradient clipping at 1, EMA 0.999, 10% of labels dropped for classifier-free guidance, seed 0, float32,  steps. It took  s ( steps/s) against the DDPM's 906.7 s, measured: the objective costs nothing extra.




Validation loss of the trained (EMA) model by time t, on 2,048 validation images with fresh noise, measured. The loss is a regression onto a partly random target, so it has a floor that depends on t. At t = 0 the input is the noise itself and only the image is unknown; given the class, a Fashion-MNIST image varies little per pixel (most pixels are background), so the loss is . At t = 1 the input is the clean image and the target still contains the noise it came from, which the image says nothing about: the loss is , about the noise's variance of 1. It is lowest in the middle ( at t = 0.5). A low loss does not mean good samples; score samples instead (sections 3 and 4).


Go deeper (optional): the derivation (why regressing on per-pair velocities gives the marginal field) and the general Gaussian-path family are on the Variational inference and generative-model maths page; the child page Flow matching takes this further.






3. Sampling is solving an ODE: Euler, Heun, midpoint


The problem. The network gives a velocity at any (x, t); turning that into a sample means integrating dx/dt = vθ(x, t) from t = 0 to 1. A computer does it in finite steps, and every step costs one or more network evaluations (NFE, the number of function evaluations, is the real cost: each is a full forward pass).


How it works. Euler: move along the current velocity for a step of size h; one evaluation per step; its error shrinks in proportion to h (first order). Heun: take the Euler step as a guess, evaluate the velocity there too, and step with the average of the two slopes. Midpoint: evaluate at the half step and use that slope. Both cost two evaluations a step and their error shrinks with h² (second order). Adaptive solvers such as dopri5 pick h themselves (Meta's library defaults to Euler and lists dopri5, midpoint and heun3 from torchdiffeq: flow_matching/solver/ode_solver.py lines 34 and 70). The samplers this lab ran, from src/flow/fm_samplers.py (the Heun variant with a last Euler step is in the same file):




Integration error against a fine solution, at equal cost




Root-mean-square pixel difference from the fine answer, 200 images (20 per class), the trained image model, measured. Both axes logarithmic: the slopes are the solvers' orders. The reference is midpoint with 500 steps, which never evaluates t = 1. At  evaluations Euler is  away, plain Heun , midpoint , Heun with a last Euler step  (9 evaluations). Even midpoint's error stops falling past 50 evaluations ( at 50,  at 100): finer steps evaluate closer to t = 1, where the field is rough.


The cost, and a surprise. A second-order step costs two evaluations, so compare at equal NFE. On the image model the midpoint solver wins clearly: FD  at 4 evaluations against Euler's , and one midpoint step (2 evaluations) scores  against  for two Euler steps. Plain Heun is far worse than both ( at 4 evaluations). The culprit is its last corrector, which evaluates the network at t = 1. There the input is a clean image and the noise it came from is independent of it, so the best squared-error answer is v = x1 − E[x0] = the input itself, not the slope of any path: measured on 1,000 validation images, the net's output at t = 1 has cosine  with its input and  with the true x1 − x0 (at t = 0.9: ). Make Heun's last step plain Euler, as diffusers' HeunDiscreteScheduler does (v0.41.0, scheduling_heun_discrete.py lines 364 and 367: no corrector on the final interval, so n steps cost 2n − 1 evaluations), and it recovers:  at 5 evaluations,  at 9. On the toy, whose modes have width and so no such sharp end, the ranking is the textbook one: at 4 evaluations Euler lands  of the points on a mode, Heun , midpoint ; at 2 evaluations a single second-order step loses to two Euler steps ( and  against ).


Toy: recorded scores by steps (2,000 points, Python, the same quantised networks the page runs)






Euler for the flow models, DDIM for diffusion. W2 (the 2-Wasserstein distance, computed by optimal assignment between 2,000 samples and 2,000 data points) is  between two sets of real samples: below about that, differences are noise. Straightness of the fine paths (distance over path length; 1 = straight): random pairs , diffusion DDIM , OT pairs , after reflow . In 2-D the crossing of random pairs bends the flow more than the diffusion arc (the Math page, section 18 found the same on two moons); on images it is the other way round (section 4).

The comparison. Diffusion rows are the Diffusion lab's recorded runs; flow rows are this lab's. One network evaluation costs the same for both ( ms for 1,000 images, measured), so equal NFE is equal time.

Before and after: one noise, ten steps, two models


One of the Diffusion lab's starting noises (seed 21, asked for an ankle boot), ten steps, the same noise for both models. Left: where the sampler is (xt). Right: where the model thinks it will end: for flow the straight-line guess xt + (1 − t) v, for diffusion its predicted clean image x̂0.

diffusion, DDIM






Why flow needs fewer steps here. Three reasons, measured or derived on this pair of models. (1) Path shape. Measured over 50 steps on 200 images, the flow model's paths have straightness  (distance over path length; 1 = straight) against  for DDIM on the diffusion model. Even with a perfect denoiser, the DDPM path xt = √ā x0 + √(1 − ā) ε traces an arc (the two coefficients stay on a unit circle), whose chord over length is about 2√2/π ≈ 0.90 for a quarter circle (derived); the straight path has no such built-in bend, and in 1,024 dimensions the crossing of random pairs bends it only a little. (2) Where the steps fall. DDIM on the linear DDPM schedule spends its steps evenly in timestep, but most of that schedule is nearly pure noise (signal below noise from t = 259 of 1,000, the Diffusion lab, section 2), so few steps leave few for the part that shapes the image; flow's uniform t spends half its steps where the image is more than half formed. (3) The prediction. Near pure noise, recovering x̂0 from a noise prediction divides by √āt (0.0064 at the last timestep), which amplifies errors, while a velocity stays bounded: one DDIM step lands  (RMS per pixel) from the 50-step answer, one flow Euler step . Straightness is not the whole story: on the 2-D toy the random-pair flow is less straight than DDIM ( against , as the Math page, section 18 found on two moons) and still needs fewer steps. A better diffusion schedule or sampler closes much of the gap (DPM-Solver++ in the Diffusion lab; the flow schedule written as diffusion in section 6).


Where diffusion still wins here. 







5. Straighter paths: reflow and distillation


The problem. One-step generation needs paths so straight that a single Euler step follows them. Section 2 showed why plain flow matching does not give that: random pairs cross, and the averaged field bends.


How it works. Reflow (Liu et al. 2022): sample many noises z, solve the trained flow's ODE to get X1 = flow(z), and train again with the same loss on the fixed pairs (z, X1) instead of random pairs. Paths of an ODE never cross, so the new pairs never cross, and the new averaged field is (nearly) the straight line for each pair. Repeating it gives the 3-rectified flow and so on. Distillation then trains a student to jump from z to X1 in one evaluation. The pairs are fixed and deterministic, which is why the toy's reflow loss falls to  against  for random pairs (that floor is the variance of the random target).


Measured here.  pairs from the flow model (midpoint, 25 steps, the converged ODE by section 3's scores;  s on MPS; a first set made with plain Heun was discarded because of its inaccurate end points; the pairs are kept unclamped, as the ODE's exact map, so  of their pixels lie outside [−1, 1]), then  more training steps from the first model on those pairs ( s), same recipe otherwise. 




Published, at scale. Liu et al.'s CIFAR-10 table (unconditional, Table 1, published): one Euler step gives FID 378 for the 1-rectified flow and 12.21 after one reflow (8.15 after two); adding distillation, 6.18 and 4.85. With the adaptive RK45 solver the order flips: 2.58 (127 evaluations) for the 1-rectified flow against 3.36 (110) after reflow. Reflow buys few-step quality and costs a little full-solve quality, because the pairs carry the first model's errors (on the toy:  on a mode at 64 steps before reflow,  after). InstaFlow (Liu et al. 2023) applies reflow then distillation to Stable Diffusion: one step, FID 23.3 on MS COCO 2017-5k, 13.1 on MS COCO 2014-30k in 0.09 s, for 199 A100 GPU-days of training (abstract, published). Minibatch OT pairing (Tong et al. 2023) straightens the paths during the first training instead (the toy's OT pairs model); in high dimensions a batch of a few hundred images is a weak approximation of the full transport plan, so it helps less there than on a 2-D toy.


When it matters. Reflow and distillation are what let flow models sample in 1 to 4 steps: FLUX.1 [schnell] is "a 12 billion parameter rectified flow transformer" that generates in "1 to 4 steps", distilled with latent adversarial diffusion distillation (model card, published). For a model you train yourself, reflow costs a pair-generation pass plus a second training; check it by FD at 1, 2 and 4 steps before and after, and at many steps to see what it cost.






6. One family: flow, diffusion and the probability-flow ODE


The idea. Both models train on the same kind of input: a scaled image plus scaled Gaussian noise, xt = at · image + bt · noise. The DDPM schedule uses a = √āt, b = √(1 − āt) (variance preserving); the straight path uses a = t, b = 1 − t. Any such model can be read as predicting the noise, the clean image or the velocity, because given xt each determines the others. With this lab's convention (t = 0 noise, derived from xt = (1 − t) x0 + t x1 and v = x1 − x0):


x̂1 = xt + (1 − t) vθ,   x̂0 (the noise) = xt − t vθ


Every diffusion model also has a deterministic ODE with the same marginals at every t, the probability-flow ODE (Song et al. 2021), and DDIM is a way to solve it. So "flow matching against diffusion" is not two kinds of model but three separable choices: the path (schedule), what the network outputs (which sets how the loss weighs each noise level) and how t is drawn in training. The blog Diffusion Meets Flow Matching: Two Sides of the Same Coin (diffusionflow.github.io; its acknowledgements thank colleagues at Google DeepMind; authors and date not shown on the page, read 2026-10-17) puts it as "diffusion models and Gaussian flow matching are the same", and shows that DDIM on the flow schedule is exactly the flow Euler step ("Diffusion with DDIM sampler == Flow matching sampler (Euler)"). The Diffusion lab saw the same identity from the other side: diffusers' Euler sampler and DDIM gave the same FD within 0.2 on its model.


The convention trap, at the pinned version. diffusers' flow scheduler counts the other way: σ = 1 is noise. FlowMatchEulerDiscreteScheduler (diffusers v0.41.0, schedulers/scheduling_flow_match_euler_discrete.py) noises with sample = sigma * noise + (1.0 - sigma) * sample (line 234), so its model output is noise − image (the negative of this lab's v); it steps with dt = sigma_next - sigma (line 504, negative) and prev_sample = sample + dt * model_output (line 511), and the timestep it passes the network is sigmas * num_train_timesteps, σ × 1000 (line 367). Same maths, opposite sign and a factor of 1,000 on t: section 9 shows what each mix-up does.


Timestep shift. Higher resolutions need more noise to destroy the same structure, so SD3 shifts the schedule towards noise: tm = √(m/n) tn / (1 + (√(m/n) − 1) tn) on the noise level, with "a shift value of α = 3.0 both during training and sampling at resolution 1024×1024" (Esser et al. 2024, section 5.3.2, eq. 23, published); diffusers implements it as sigmas = self.shift * sigmas / (1 + (self.shift - 1) * sigmas) (line 351), and Z-Image-Turbo ships shift 3 (the Model map). On this 28 × 28 model, at sampling time only: 


Shift at 4 steps, same noise


shift 1/3 (towards data)


no shift


shift 3 (towards noise)


Which t to train on. Uniform t is the default here. SD3 compared training-time distributions over t and found logit-normal sampling (draw u from a normal with mean m and scale s, take the logistic of it) with m = 0, s = 1 "consistently achieves a good rank" across their settings (section 5.1.1 and Table 1, published): it spends more training on the middle of the path, where the per-t loss is neither trivially easy nor pure guesswork. Not run here: it needs a second 15-minute training to show a difference smaller than the noise of a 1,000-sample FD.


Go deeper (optional): the probability-flow ODE and score matching are derived on the Math page, sections 15, 16 and 18; noise schedules and SNR in the Diffusion lab, section 2.







7. Guidance works the same way


Classifier-free guidance needs nothing new: the model was trained with 10% of labels dropped, so it gives a conditional velocity vc and an unconditional vu, and the sampler uses vu + s (vc − vu) (diffusers' convention: s = 1 is the plain conditional model, s = 0 unconditional; SD3's pipeline applies the same line to its flow transformer's output, pipelines/stable_diffusion_3/pipeline_stable_diffusion_3.py line 1083 at v0.41.0). Two evaluations per step, so a guided 50-step sample costs 100 evaluations.

Choosing, in one paragraph. For a new image or video generator trained from scratch, flow matching on straight paths is the default: one line of loss, no schedule to tune beyond a shift, good few-step behaviour, and it composes with every trick diffusion has (guidance, latent spaces, distillation, higher-order or multistep solvers). Diffusion with ε prediction remains the right reading for the large body of existing checkpoints and tools (SD 1.5, SDXL). Neither choice fixes cost by itself: steps do, and step counts of 1 to 4 come from distillation, not from the objective. Autoregressive generation is the other option (the Reading tab compares it).






9. Debugging a flow model


Two bugs reproduced on the trained model (Euler, 50 steps, same noise), then the mistakes that do not crash but mislead.


Two convention bugs, measured (first five classes shown)


correct


time reversed


t × 1000




Samples are blurry class averages
Too few steps for curved paths: the first steps follow the average direction (section 2). Check FD and diversity against steps; if quality appears only at 10+ steps and you need fewer, reflow or distil (section 5) rather than tuning the solver.


Comparing solvers at equal steps, or evaluating the net at the data end
Heun and midpoint cost two evaluations per step: compare at equal NFE (section 3). And a solver that evaluates the network at exactly t = 1 (plain Heun's last corrector) uses a slope the model cannot know; on this lab's images that made Heun worse than Euler. End with an Euler step, or use a solver that never touches the endpoint (midpoint).


Reading the training loss as quality
The flow-matching loss has a floor set by the randomness of the target (about 1 near t = 1, where the noise must be guessed from a clean image) and says little about samples. Score samples (FD at a fixed sample size, class accuracy, diversity) at several step counts.


Mixing the t = 0 and t = 1 conventions, or the sign of v
Lipman et al. and this lab: t = 0 is noise, v = data − noise. diffusers: σ = 1 is noise, output = noise − data, σ × 1000 into the net. Porting a checkpoint between the two needs both the time flip and the sign flip; either one alone produces the garbage above.


Expecting reflow to be free
The pairs inherit the first model's mistakes, so full-solve quality can drop slightly (Liu et al.'s CIFAR-10 RK45 FID 2.58 to 3.36; the toy at 64 steps). Measure both ends: few-step and many-step.


Copying a guidance scale or a shift between models
Both depend on the model, resolution and step count: SD3's shift 3.0 is for 1024 × 1024; on this 28 × 28 model the best shift and guidance are different (sections 6 and 7). Sweep them on a few hundred samples.







10. Interview questions


What does a flow-matching model predict, and what is its loss?
A velocity vθ(xt, t). Training: xt = (1 − t) noise + t data, loss ‖vθ − (data − noise)‖², t uniform (or logit-normal). Sampling: integrate dx/dt = v from noise to data.


Why is it called simulation-free, and why does that matter?
Training never solves the ODE: each step builds xt in closed form from a random pair and does one regression. Older continuous normalizing flows had to simulate the ODE (and backpropagate through it) every step, which made them slow to train.


Each training path is a straight line. Why are the sampled paths curved?
The network learns the average of all straight lines passing through each (x, t); pairs cross, so the average direction changes along a path. On the toy, random-pair paths have straightness  (1 = straight), reflowed ones .


Are flow matching and diffusion different models?
Same family: Gaussian paths between data and noise, a network that can be read as predicting noise, data or velocity, and a deterministic ODE for sampling (DDIM solves the diffusion model's). They differ in the schedule, the output parameterisation (hence loss weighting) and the t distribution, which change which errors are cheap and how many steps are needed.


Why did the flow model need fewer steps than the DDPM in this lab?
Three things: the DDPM path is an arc by construction (straightness about 0.90 even with a perfect model; measured  against  for flow); the linear schedule is nearly pure noise for most of its range, so evenly spaced steps waste most of their budget; and x̂0 from an ε prediction divides by a tiny √ā at the noisy end, while a velocity stays bounded. Straightness alone does not decide it: on the 2-D toy the flow was less straight than DDIM and still needed fewer steps.


What is reflow and what does it cost?
Generate (noise, sample) pairs with the trained flow, retrain on them: the pairs do not cross, so the new paths are nearly straight and 1 to 2 Euler steps work. Cost: a generation pass over many pairs and a second training; the pairs carry the first model's errors, so many-step quality can drop slightly. Usually followed by distillation for one step.


Design: your product needs a 4-step image generator; you have a 50-step flow model.
Options, cheapest first: tune the solver and shift at 4 steps (minutes; limited gain); a second-order or multistep solver at equal NFE; reflow then 4-step Euler (one pair pass plus a fine-tune); distillation into a few-step student (progressive, consistency or adversarial, as FLUX.1 [schnell]'s latent adversarial diffusion distillation); drop CFG at inference by distilling it in (halves evaluations). Measure FD or a preference score at 4 steps against the 50-step teacher, plus time per image including the VAE decode.


Euler or Heun?
Compare at equal network evaluations. Second-order solvers' error falls with h², so they usually win from moderate budgets up, but how the solver treats the data end matters as much: on this lab's images midpoint won at every budget, while plain Heun lost to Euler until its last step was made Euler (it evaluates the net at t = 1, where the learned field is just the input). With guidance each evaluation is already two forward passes, so a second-order step with CFG costs four.


A flow model that trained fine samples garbage. What do you check?
Time direction (which end is noise), the scale of t passed to the network ([0, 1] or ×1000), the sign of the velocity, the shift and step grid, the null label for guidance, and dtype. Then one known-good test: the 1-step output should be a recognisable blur of the class; if it is not, the convention is wrong, not the model.
