How a model turns pixels into something it can compare with words, from zero, on real weights: CLIP ViT-B/32 and SigLIP 2 base (patch 16), run here on the topic’s running example (the 16 colour test images and the 10,000 Fashion-MNIST test images). Every number marked measured was computed for this page on an Apple M1 Pro, on the CPU (float32, 4 threads), on 2026-10-17; published numbers are quoted from the paper that states them; derived numbers show their formula.


1. Patches2. Convolutions and attention3. Contrastive training4. Zero-shot5. What embeddings miss6. Mistakes and questions


In one screen


    

  • A vision transformer cuts an image into square patches, turns each into a vector with one shared matrix, adds a learned position vector, and from then on treats the image as a sequence of tokens, like words.
    • 

  • CLIP and SigLIP train an image tower and a text tower together so that a picture and its caption land close together. CLIP uses a softmax over the whole batch; SigLIP judges every image-caption pair on its own with a sigmoid, which needs no batch-wide sum and so shards more cheaply.
    • 

  • That shared space gives zero-shot classification: write one sentence per class, pick the nearest. On Fashion-MNIST it works far above chance but well below a probe trained on a few hundred labels: the information is in the embedding, the prompts only get part of it out.
    • 

  • The embedding keeps what helps match captions and loses much else: a written word can override the object, and counting, left and right, and which colour belongs to which shape are close to guesses.
    • 



Models: openai/clip-vit-base-patch32 at revision 3d74acf9a28c and google/siglip2-base-patch16-224 at revision 75de2d55ec2d, through transformers 5.20.1 (loaders pinned in the root’s src/data/pretrained.py). Licences, parameter counts and the 16 test images are in the root’s running example (src/data/README.md). The papers have their own pages with trained toys: ViT and CLIP; this lab does not repeat them, it runs the real released models.





1. An image as a sequence of patches


The problem. A transformer reads a sequence of vectors. An image is a grid of pixels: 224 × 224 × 3 = 150,528 numbers. Treating every pixel as a token would give 50,176 tokens and about 2.5 billion attention scores per head per layer derived: 224² = 50,176; 50,176², far too many. The Vision Transformer (ViT, Dosovitskiy et al., October 2020) groups pixels into square patches instead: its title, “An Image is Worth 16x16 Words”, is the patch size.


How it works. Cut the image into a grid of P × P patches; unroll each into a vector of 3P² numbers; multiply every one by the same learned matrix (the patch embedding) to get a token of width D (768 for both models here); add a learned position embedding, one vector per slot, so the model can tell where each patch was; optionally prepend a learned summary token, [CLS]; run the transformer; and pool the output into one image vector, either by taking the [CLS] output (CLIP) or with a small attention layer whose learned query looks at every patch (SigLIP’s MAP head, multihead attention pooling). Watch both models do it to the same image:













Everything drawn is real: the patches are the model’s 224-pixel input, the token colours are the first 8 of 768 numbers each model’s patch embedding produces for this image, the position similarities come from the released position-embedding table, and the last step shows where each model’s pooling looks measured. On SigLIP 2’s fixed pooling slots compare Vision Transformers Need Registers (Darcet et al., September 2023): “high-norm tokens appearing during inference primarily in low-informative background areas of images, that are repurposed for internal computations”. SigLIP 2 B/16 has such tokens too: the child page Vision encoders measured three patch tokens, at fixed grid positions, with 15 to 23 times the median norm in every image measured. Switch the model to see the same image as 49 coarse tokens or 196 fine ones.




“A convolution” is just this matrix. Both models implement the patch embedding as a 2-D convolution with kernel size and stride equal to the patch size, which is the same arithmetic as cutting, flattening and multiplying. The check below cuts the five images above into patches with unfold, multiplies by the convolution’s own weights reshaped into a matrix, and compares with the model’s convolution (from src/vision/analyse.py; output from the run):


conv = emb.patch_embedding(pv).flatten(2).transpose(1, 2)                         # the model's own way
cols = torch.nn.functional.unfold(pv, kernel_size=ps, stride=ps).transpose(1, 2)  # cut and flatten
W = emb.patch_embedding.weight.reshape(emb.patch_embedding.weight.shape[0], -1)   # one matrix
mm = cols @ W.T + (emb.patch_embedding.bias if emb.patch_embedding.bias is not None else 0)
print((mm - conv).abs().max())


Output: 0.0 for CLIP (a 768 × 3,072 matrix, no bias, 2,359,296 parameters) and 6.9e-06 for SigLIP 2 (768 × 768 plus a bias, 590,592 parameters), float32 rounding measured. The convolution is the efficient way to write “cut, flatten, multiply”; nothing convolutional happens across patches.


The cost. Tokens grow with the square of resolution over patch size: N = (224 / P)², and attention per layer grows with N². Halving the patch from 32 to 16 quadruples the tokens (49 to 196) and multiplies attention scores by about 15 (2,500 to 38,416 with CLIP’s [CLS]) derived. That is the same trade a vision-language model makes when it decides how many image tokens to put in a prompt (VLM lab). On the CPU here CLIP B/32 embedded 119 Fashion-MNIST images per second (15,000 in 126 s) and SigLIP 2 B/16 23 per second (15,000 in 654 s) measured; a 5.2× gap; part of it is the 4× token count, part the different software paths, so the ratio is not a clean measure of either.


When it matters, how to check. Fine detail (small text, thin lines, counting small things) needs small patches or higher resolution; a 32-pixel patch sees a whole word as one blob. Check a model’s patch_size and image_size in its config.json, and what its processor does to your image (CLIP resizes the short side to 224 and centre-crops, so a wide image loses its edges; SigLIP 2’s processor squashes to 224 × 224 without cropping).







2. Convolutions against attention, and learning without captions


Inductive bias. A convolutional network (CNN) slides small filters (3 × 3 pixels, say) over the image, so each layer only mixes neighbours and the same filter is used everywhere. Those two built-in assumptions (nearby pixels belong together; a pattern means the same thing anywhere) are its inductive bias: they make it learn from little data, and they limit what one layer can see. A stack of L such layers (stride 1) sees a window of only 2L + 1 pixels derived; real CNNs downsample to see further. A ViT has neither assumption: from the first layer every patch can attend to every other, and it must learn locality from data. The ViT paper found that this costs it on small datasets and pays off at scale: it beat the best CNNs of 2020 only after pre-training on hundreds of millions of images (the ViT page animates one image through a ViT and a ResNet and retrains both at toy scale). The position-similarity step above shows the learned version of locality in released weights: nobody told either model that the grid is 2-D.


Learning without captions. Labels are scarce, so most vision encoders are pre-trained on a proxy task. Self-supervised methods use the images alone. MAE masks “a high proportion of the input image, e.g., 75%” of the patches and learns to reconstruct the missing pixels, running the encoder on the visible patches only (He et al., November 2021). DINO trains a student network to match a slowly updated teacher copy of itself across different crops of the same image, “a form of self-distillation with no labels”, and its ViT features turn out to contain “explicit information about the semantic segmentation of an image” (Caron et al., April 2021). These give strong features for dense tasks (segmentation, depth, matching) but no link to words; image-text training (next section) gives that link. SigLIP 2 combines both: it adds “captioning-based pretraining, self-supervised losses (self-distillation, masked prediction) and online data curation” to the sigmoid loss (Tschannen et al., February 2025). Collapse, MAE against I-JEPA and InfoNCE on a real text batch are taught on Contrastive and self-supervised learning.






3. Contrastive image-text training: CLIP’s softmax and SigLIP’s sigmoid


The problem. We want an image vector and a text vector that can be compared directly, so that “a photo of a cat” lands near cat photos. There are hundreds of millions of image-caption pairs on the web but no labels saying how similar any two are. Contrastive training uses the pairing itself as the label: in a batch of N pairs, each image’s own caption is the positive and the other N − 1 captions are negatives.


How it works. Two towers (a ViT for images, a transformer for text) each end in a vector; both are scaled to length 1, so their dot product is the cosine similarity (1 for the same direction, 0 for unrelated). Multiply every cosine by a learned scale t (the inverse of the temperature) to get logits, then:


CLIP: ℓ = ½ [ CErows(t · S) + CEcolumns(t · S) ]


SigLIP: ℓ = −(1/N) Σi,j log σ( zij (t · Sij + b) )


S
the N × N matrix of cosines, images in rows, captions in columns; the diagonal holds the true pairs


CE
cross-entropy of a softmax with the diagonal as the right answer: each image must pick its caption out of the row, each caption its image out of the column (this is the InfoNCE loss)


t, b
learned scale and (SigLIP only) bias; SigLIP learns t′ = log t and initialises t′ and b “to log 10 and −10 respectively”, so training starts from the prior that almost every pair is a mismatch (Zhai et al. 2023, §3.2)


zij
+1 on the diagonal, −1 elsewhere: every cell is a separate yes-or-no question


σ
the logistic sigmoid 1 / (1 + e−x)


In transformers 5.20.1 these are a few lines: CLIP’s contrastive_loss is a cross-entropy against torch.arange(len(logits)) (models/clip/modeling_clip.py:47), applied to the logits and their transpose and averaged; SigLIP’s logits are logits_per_text * logit_scale.exp() + logit_bias (models/siglip/modeling_siglip.py:805) and the loss is logsigmoid(m1_diag1 * logits_per_text) summed over each row and averaged (:814), with m1_diag1 the ±1 label matrix. CLIP’s scale started at 1 / 0.07 and was clipped at 100 (CLIP paper §2.5, quoted on the CLIP page); the released B/32 sits exactly at that clip, t = 100.0, and SigLIP 2 learned t = 112.67 with b = −16.77 read from the weights in float32.



The real 16 × 16 matrix


The 16 colour test images against their own 16 captions, through each released model. Click a cell for its numbers; switch the view to see the same cosines as CLIP’s row and column softmaxes or as SigLIP’s independent sigmoids.














Rows: the 16 test images (p01 to p04 photographs, s01 to s06 synthetic scenes, g01 to g06 generated by SD 1.5). Columns: their captions, numbered in the same order (hover a number for the text). measured




What the matrix shows measured. CLIP B/32 puts the right caption first for 15 of 16 images; its one miss is the typographic image s04 (“the cat photo with a white sticker reading DOG”), which it matches to the plain cat caption instead. SigLIP 2 gets all 16, but only after its text is lowercased, as the SigLIP 2 reference code does (its demo notebook preprocesses text with lower(key="text") before tokenising; big_vision commit 0127fb6b337e, SigLIP2_demo.ipynb). Fed the captions with their capitals, as the transformers processor alone does, it also misses s04 (15 of 16), whose caption contains “DOG” in capitals. Cosines are low in absolute terms: CLIP’s matching pairs average 0.333 and its other pairs 0.166; SigLIP 2’s average 0.194 and −0.019. The softmax view shows CLIP’s choice among 16 is confident even so, because the scale of 100 turns a gap of 0.05 in cosine into a factor of e5 ≈ 150 in probability.



The loss on a real batch: temperature and batch size


Take the first N of those pairs as a batch and compute both losses from the real cosines. Move the scale and the batch size.


Predict first: as the scale t goes to 0, what does the softmax loss tend to? And as t grows very large?
At t = 0 every logit is 0, every softmax is uniform, and the loss is exactly ln N whatever the embeddings: the chance level. As t grows the softmax approaches an argmax: rows the model gets right cost almost nothing, but a row where a negative beats the positive costs about t times the gap, so the loss is dominated by the hardest negatives. A learned temperature settles between: sharp enough to separate, soft enough to keep gradients from all negatives. On the first 8 pairs (which include the typographic image s04), the CLIP softmax loss falls from ln 8 = 2.079 at t = 1 to its minimum, 0.071, near t = 100 (the learned value) and rises again to 0.121 at t = 316, because the one wrong row (s04) is punished more and more. On SigLIP 2’s embeddings, where all 8 rows are right, the softmax loss just keeps falling as t grows measured.



















The curve: this batch’s loss at every scale (log axis), the dot at the current one. Bars: each pair’s share of the loss (for the softmax, the mean of its row and column cross-entropies; for the sigmoid, the sum over its row).






Why a big batch matters for the softmax. The loss only learns from the negatives that are in the batch, and the chance level ln N grows with the batch: a batch of 16 asks the model to pick 1 out of 16, CLIP’s batch of 32,768 asked it to pick 1 out of 32,768 (CLIP page). Hard negatives (two cats, two similar captions) only show up in large batches. That is why contrastive models were trained with huge batches, and why the cost of the softmax’s batch-wide sums matters.


Why the sigmoid scales. The softmax normalises each row and each column over the whole batch, so with the batch split over D devices every device needs every other device’s embeddings (an all-gather) and holds at least its rows of the full matrix. The sigmoid scores each cell alone, so SigLIP’s “chunked” implementation keeps each device’s images in place and passes text embeddings round the devices in D steps; “the memory cost at any given moment is reduced from |B|2 to b2”, with b = |B| / D, and “D collective permutes is typically faster than two all-gathers” (SigLIP §3.3). The calculator below applies that accounting derived from §3.3, float32 logits:












Bar length on a log scale. Embedding width 768.






What the paper measured published: with locked image features (SigLiT), “when the batch size is smaller than 16 k, sigmoid loss outperforms softmax loss by a large margin”; they trained up to a batch of one million, but “performance for both sigmoid and softmax saturate at around 32 k batch size”, and for SigLIP proper “a very large batch size hurts both losses” (SigLIP §4.1 and Figure 2). With only four TPUv4 chips a SigLiT model reached 84.5% ImageNet zero-shot in two days (abstract). So the sigmoid’s advantage is mostly cost and small-batch quality, not a higher ceiling. Not run here: training either loss at scale; the calculator only evaluates both on released embeddings, and the CLIP embeddings were trained with the softmax, the SigLIP 2 ones with the sigmoid, so a loss computed with the other model’s rule says nothing about how that model would have trained.


Go deeper (optional): a toy CLIP trained from scratch, its batch with a temperature slider and an animated softmax-against-sigmoid on the CLIP page; InfoNCE before and after training on real text, and the temperature’s effect on hard negatives, on Contrastive and self-supervised learning.






4. Zero-shot classification: a classifier written in sentences


How it works. Write one sentence per class (“a photo of a sneaker.”), embed the ten sentences once with the text tower, embed the image, and pick the class whose sentence has the highest cosine. No training on the task: the ten text vectors are the classifier’s weights. In code, from src/vision/zeroshot.py (embeddings unit length):


s = et @ T[k].T          # [10,000 test images] x [10 class sentences] cosines
pred = s.argmax(1)       # nearest sentence wins
acc = (pred == yt).mean()


The test. Fashion-MNIST, the topic’s running example: 10,000 grey 28 × 28 test images of clothing, 1,000 per class, upscaled by each processor to 224. These look nothing like web photos, which makes them a fair test of transfer. Two class wordings (the dataset’s official names, such as “T-shirt/top”, and plain ones, such as “t-shirt”) times five templates, plus the average of the five template embeddings (prompt ensembling, which the CLIP paper used), all measured.












20 test images: the first two of each class, in class order (T-shirt/top, trouser, pullover, dress, coat, sandal, shirt, sneaker, bag, ankle boot). Cosines recorded from the real models; the page only applies the softmax.




Every prompt set on all 10,000 test images




What the table shows measured. Chance is 10%. CLIP B/32 lands between 61.3% and 66.7% whatever the wording: the template moves it by about 5 points, and the ensemble (64.8%) is not its best. Its tokenizer lowercases everything, so “official” and “official, lowercased” are identical. SigLIP 2 B/16 reaches 74.5% with plain names and the ensemble, the best of any set, but scores 20.0% to 22.8% with the official names as written: the capital letters in “T-shirt/top”, “Trouser”, “Pullover” (tokenised as Trou, ser and Pull, over instead of tr, ouser and pullover) send it far from the lowercase text it was trained on. Lowercasing the same names brings it back to 66.9% to 73.1%. A cross-check with one template (“a photo of a ….”) isolates the cause: SigLIP 2 scores 22.3% with official names, 70.2% lowercased, 72.9% with plain names and 22.4% with the plain names capitalised; CLIP scores 63.3%, 63.3%, 61.3% and 61.3% (diag_case.py). A silent preprocessing difference cost 50 points.












The errors are the ones a person would make, and they show what the text side cannot separate. CLIP’s best set sends 564 of 1,000 coats and 438 of 1,000 shirts to “pullover” and gets only 6.6% of shirts right; SigLIP 2’s best set gets 66% of shirts but sends 453 coats to “pullover” and 392 T-shirts to “shirt”. At 28 pixels, grey, a shirt, a pullover and a coat differ by collar and buttons, and their names overlap in web captions. With the capitalised official names SigLIP 2 calls 5,725 of the 10,000 images “T-shirt/top”: one class name absorbs everything, the signature of a text embedding gone wrong rather than an image embedding.


The embedding knows more than the prompts get out


Predict first: a linear classifier trained on the frozen image embeddings with only 16 labelled images per class (160 in all). Better or worse than the best zero-shot prompt set?
Better, for both. With 16 labels per class a linear probe reaches 79.0% on CLIP features (best prompt set 66.7%) and 84.0% on SigLIP 2 features (74.5%). Even one label per class (10 images) roughly matches zero-shot on average (58.8% and 62.2%) but swings by 15 to 16 points between draws of which ten images are labelled.




Linear probe: multinomial logistic regression on the frozen, centred embeddings, trained on k labelled validation images per class (5 random draws for k ≤ 64; the black line spans the worst and best draw), tested on the same 10,000 test images. Reference: the topic’s small CNN classifier, 550,890 parameters, trained from scratch for two minutes on all 55,000 training images (root’s smoke test). measured


Reading it measured. With 500 labels per class the probe reaches 87.8% (CLIP) and 89.3% (SigLIP 2): the class information is in the frozen image embedding, and ten sentences extract only part of it. A 550,890-parameter CNN trained from scratch on 55,000 labelled images for two minutes still wins (92.98%): with enough in-domain labels, a small specialised model beats a general encoder, and the encoder’s value is in needing few or no labels. A mistake made on the way, worth knowing: a first probe fed the unit-length embeddings to gradient descent without rescaling (every coordinate is around 1/√768) and underfit, reporting 79.8% and 84.6% at 500 per class; dividing by the features’ standard deviation fixed it. Settings (fixed before looking at test accuracy, not tuned): full-batch gradient descent, learning rate 0.5, L2 1e-3, 1,000 steps. Published comparison: none; the CLIP paper’s tables (transcribed on the CLIP page) include MNIST but not Fashion-MNIST, so these numbers stand on their own and are not a benchmark of either model.







5. What the embeddings capture, and what they miss


A contrastive embedding keeps whatever helps pick the right caption out of a batch of web captions, and nothing else. Web captions name objects and often repeat the text written in the picture; they rarely state counts, left and right, or which attribute goes with which object. So the embedding is strong on “what is it” and “what does it say”, and weak on structure. Researchers found CLIP-like models behave partly like bags of words on such questions (Yuksekgonul et al. 2022), and OpenAI called the first failure below a typographic attack, noting it needs “no more technology than pen and paper” (OpenAI, March 2021, archived).


The typographic attack: the same cat, before and after a sticker












Images: the scikit-image cat photo (CC0) with a white label drawn by src/vision/make_probes.py; the DOG version is the root’s test image s04. Four texts: a photo of a cat, dog, bird, car. measured




What it shows measured. CLIP B/32 flips from cat to the written word for DOG (cosine 0.2855 for dog against 0.2775 for cat) and for BIRD (0.2837 against 0.2659), whether the DOG sticker is small or large; it resists CAR, narrowly (cat 0.2890, car 0.2827). The CAT sticker raises the cat score (0.2926 against 0.2846 plain): the written word adds to the image’s meaning in the same direction as the object. SigLIP 2 never flips, but the sticker still moves it: “dog” rises from 0.0684 to 0.1112 with the DOG sticker while “cat” stays near 0.13. Both models read text; SigLIP 2’s image of the cat is strong enough to win. These numbers match the root’s float16 smoke test on the DOG image to within 0.0001 in cosine. The VLM lab asks SmolVLM the same question in words: it answered “There is a cat in this image.” (root smoke test).


Counting, left and right, binding




What it shows measured. Counting: CLIP gets 3 of 6 (one, three and six), calls two “three” and four and five “six”, with margins of 0.001 to 0.008 in cosine; SigLIP 2 gets 4 of 6 (one to three, and six), calling four “five” and five “six”, with larger margins on the small counts (0.02 to 0.03). Small counts of simple shapes are within reach of the newer model, larger ones are not; six probes are a hint, not an accuracy. Left and right: both models pick the same sentence for the scene and its mirror image, so each is right once by construction, a coin toss; the margins are a few thousandths. Binding: CLIP gets both swapped-colour scenes wrong; SigLIP 2 picks the same sentence for both. The sentences contain the same words in a different order, and the embeddings barely see the order. Larger sets of such minimal pairs (Winoground, ARO) found the same for many CLIP-like models.


How to check a model for these. Build minimal pairs: two images that differ in one property (a sticker, a mirror flip, swapped colours) or two captions that differ in one word, and see whether the score moves the right way. Count how often the right one wins and how large the margin is; a margin of a few thousandths of a cosine is a coin toss. Benchmarks built this way exist (Winoground, ARO, SugarCrepe), and VLM-level versions are on Long-context and multimodal benchmarks. The fix is usually not a better prompt: it is training data with hard negatives (captions with swapped words), a model that reads the image tokens with a language model (VLM lab), or both.







6. Common mistakes and interview questions


Comparing raw cosines across models
CLIP’s matching pairs here sit around 0.3 and SigLIP 2’s around 0.1 to 0.2; neither number means “30% similar”. Only the order within one model is meaningful, and thresholds (for retrieval or filtering) must be calibrated per model.


Feeding SigLIP text the way CLIP is fed
Two traps. Case: SigLIP 2’s reference code lowercases text before tokenising, the transformers processor does not, and CLIP’s tokenizer lowercases on its own, so code written for CLIP silently passes capitals to SigLIP 2; here that turned 70.2% into 22.3% on Fashion-MNIST (section 4). Padding: SigLIP was trained on text padded to a fixed 64 tokens (padding="max_length", max_length=64 in the processor call); padding to the longest in the batch, as CLIP code does, changes its text embeddings. The root’s loaders and this lab pass it explicitly.


Forgetting what the processor does to the image
CLIP resizes the short side to 224 and centre-crops (edges of a wide image vanish); SigLIP 2’s fixed-resolution processor squashes to 224 × 224; normalisation constants differ (CLIP’s ImageNet-like mean and standard deviation, SigLIP’s 0.5 and 0.5). Using one model’s preprocessing with the other’s weights degrades results silently.


Reading zero-shot accuracy as what the features know
The prompt set alone moved accuracy by many points here, and a linear probe on 16 labels per class beat every prompt set. Report the prompts with any zero-shot number, and use a linear probe to judge the features.


Applying CLIP’s softmax to SigLIP outputs, or a sigmoid to CLIP
SigLIP’s logits come with a bias and are calibrated per pair (a sigmoid gives a yes-or-no probability); CLIP’s are calibrated only relative to the other candidates (softmax). A sigmoid of 100 × cosine is near 1 for every CLIP pair.


Trusting attention maps as explanations
The pooling heat in the patch animation shows where one layer’s weights go, averaged over heads; outputs mix information across all tokens in earlier layers, so a patch with low weight can still decide the answer.


Interview questions


How many tokens does a ViT-B/16 make from a 224 × 224 image, and what happens at 448?
(224/16)² = 196 (plus [CLS] if it has one). At 448: 784, so attention per layer costs 16 times as much; the learned position table must be interpolated to the new grid (transformers’ interpolate_pos_encoding) or the model fine-tuned at the new size.


Why does CLIP need large batches, and how does SigLIP change that?
The softmax’s negatives are the rest of the batch, and chance loss is ln N; hard negatives appear only in large batches. The sigmoid treats each pair as binary classification, needs no batch-wide normalisation, works better at small batches, and allows a chunked implementation holding b × b logits per device instead of the full matrix; both saturate around 32k in the SigLIP paper.


What does the temperature do, and why learn it?
It sets how peaked the softmax is. Too high a temperature (small scale): loss near ln N and weak gradients; too low: only the hardest negatives matter and training is unstable (CLIP clipped its scale at 100). Learning it lets the model sharpen as its embeddings separate.


Zero-shot accuracy is poor on your domain. What do you try, in order?
Check preprocessing; try class wordings and templates and an ensemble; measure a linear probe on a few labels per class (if it is much higher, the features are fine and you need labels or prompt tuning); if the probe is also poor, fine-tune or pick an encoder trained on closer data.


Your image search returns cat photos for the query “dog” when the photos contain the word DOG. Why, and what do you do?
Contrastive embeddings read text in images strongly (a typographic attack). Measure it with minimal pairs; mitigate with an OCR step that detects text, models trained with such hard negatives, or re-ranking with a VLM.


CNN or ViT for a small labelled dataset?
From scratch, a CNN’s inductive bias wins on small data; in practice you start from a pretrained encoder of either kind, and pretrained ViTs (CLIP, SigLIP, DINOv2) are the default backbones for VLMs and retrieval.


What transfers to a datacenter GPU


Everything except the timings: the cosines, accuracies and probe results are properties of the released weights and would match on any hardware up to float rounding (the root’s MPS float16 smoke test and this lab’s CPU float32 run agree on the typographic cosines to four decimals). Images per second here are CPU numbers on a laptop shared with other jobs; a GPU embeds these models hundreds of times faster, and the ratio between CLIP B/32 and SigLIP 2 B/16 there follows the token count and kernel quality, not this run.


Scripts and recorded outputs: src/vision/ in the root folder (analyse.py, embed_fmnist.py, zeroshot.py, make_probes.py, make_data.py; results in out/). Reading time about 22 minutes (4,900 words at 220 a minute) plus the controls.









How a picture becomes tokens a language model can read, from zero, on a real model: SmolVLM-500M-Instruct, run here on the topic’s 16 colour test images. Every number marked measured was computed for this page on an Apple M1 Pro on 2026-10-17 (the model on the GPU through PyTorch’s MPS backend, in bfloat16, greedy decoding; the token counting on the CPU); published numbers are quoted from the paper or card that states them; derived numbers show their formula.


1. Three designs2. One image, step by step3. How many tokens4. The prompt5. Training stages6. What it gets wrong7. Cost per image8. Mistakes and questions


In one screen


    

  • A vision-language model (VLM) reads images and text and writes text. Most open ones are three parts: a vision encoder (a ViT, see the Vision lab) turns image patches into vectors, a small projector maps those vectors to the language model’s width, and they are pasted into the prompt as image tokens where a placeholder stood.
    • 

  • An image costs tokens like text does. SmolVLM-500M spends 1,088 on any square image (17 views of 64), whatever its original size; LLaVA-1.5 spends 576. Tiling buys detail with tokens, and tokens cost time and context.
    • 

  • Training is usually two stages: first align the projector with everything else frozen, then instruction-tune projector and language model on conversations about images.
    • 

  • The failures are measurable. On 30 questions with known answers and 72 yes/no object questions, this small model answers 26 of 30 at the default budget (24 at 64 tokens) and says yes to 2 of 47 absent objects, but miscounts, misreads the clock and adds wrongly; its long descriptions contain wrong claims for 12 of the 16 images. The vision encoder, not the language model, takes most of the time.
    • 



Model: HuggingFaceTB/SmolVLM-500M-Instruct at revision a7da5b986cb5 (Apache 2.0; 507,482,304 parameters), through transformers 5.20.1 (loader pinned in the root’s src/data/pretrained.py). Code quoted with file and line is transformers v5.20.1. The test images, their licences and ground truth are in the root’s running example (src/data/README.md). The Reading tab’s section 6 gives the overview; this lab adds the mechanism and the measurements. Every VLM’s dates and licences are in the Model map; VLM benchmarks (MMMU, ChartQA, DocVQA and others) are on Long-context and multimodal benchmarks.





1. Three ways to give a language model eyes


The problem. A pretrained language model reads a sequence of vectors, one per token, each of a fixed width (960 numbers for SmolVLM’s language model, 4,096 for a 7B Llama). An image is a grid of pixels. Something has to turn the pixels into vectors the language model can use, without retraining it from scratch.




DesignHow the image gets inExampleCost and trade-off



Encoder + projector (“LLaVA-style”)Encoder vectors are projected to the language model’s width and placed in the sequence, as tokensLLaVA (Liu et al., April 2023), Qwen-VL, InternVL, SmolVLM, Gemma’s vision modelsSimplest; no change to the language model. Every image token takes context and attention compute.


Cross-attentionThe language model’s text tokens attend to image vectors through new layers inserted between its frozen layers; images never enter the sequenceFlamingo (Alayrac et al., April 2022); IDEFICS, its open reproductionContext stays free; the language model stays frozen. More new parameters and a less standard architecture.


Native, early fusionImages are cut into tokens (discrete codes or patches) and one transformer is trained on text and image tokens together from the startChameleon, and the unified models in the Reading tab’s section 7One model reads and can write images. Must be trained from scratch, at full cost.




Flamingo, carefully. As described in the paper (sections 2.1 to 2.3 of arXiv 2204.14198) published: a pretrained and frozen vision encoder (a Normalizer-Free ResNet); a Perceiver Resampler that “produces a fixed number of visual outputs (64)” from however many features the image or video gave; new gated cross-attention blocks inserted between the frozen language-model layers, each output multiplied by tanh(α) with α “a layer-specific learnable scalar initialized to 0”, so at the start of training the model behaves exactly like the frozen language model; and each text token “attends to the visual tokens of the image that appeared just before it”. The largest model builds on the 70B Chinchilla language model and is called Flamingo-80B; DeepMind’s announcement calls it “an 80B parameter VLM”. Flamingo was not run here; these quotes are what this page relies on.


When it matters. Since LLaVA (2023) most open VLMs use the first design, which is why this lab runs one. Cross-attention returns where images must not eat context, and Gemma 4 12B “Unified” is listed in the Model map as encoder-free (16-pixel patches go straight in), a step towards the third design.







2. One image through the model, step by step


The animation follows the cat photo through SmolVLM-500M: the colours in steps 4 and 6 are the real vectors the model computed, shown by their first three principal components (a way to squeeze 768 or 960 numbers into a red, green and blue value). The toggle runs the same image through LLaVA-1.5 as its configuration describes it (not run here).















Checked, not assumed measured: the shapes along the way are pixel values [1, 17, 3, 512, 512] → encoder [17, 1024, 768] → pixel shuffle [17, 64, 12288] → projector [17, 64, 960] → the language model’s input [1, 1142, 960]. The merged input at the 1,088 image positions equals the projected vectors exactly, in order; and output token 1 of the global view holds exactly the 16 encoder vectors of rows 0–3, columns 4–7 (compared as sets of numbers). The first three principal components shown explain 21%, 14% and 14% of the variance of the encoder vectors and 24%, 18% and 13% of the projected ones: the colours are a rough view of high-dimensional vectors, not the whole of them. Model load 4.0 s; peak GPU memory for this step 2,329 MiB.


Pixel shuffle, in plain words. The encoder gives one vector per 16-pixel patch, 1,024 per tile. Feeding all of them would cost 1,024 tokens per tile. Pixel shuffle (also called space-to-depth) takes each 4 × 4 block of neighbouring vectors and lays them side by side into one long vector: 16 × 768 = 12,288 numbers. The token count falls 16-fold to 64 while every number is kept; the projector then has to learn to read 16 positions out of one vector. The SmolVLM paper reports that “smaller VLMs benefit from more aggressive compression (r=4)” (Marafioti et al., April 2025, section 2.2) published. The code:


# transformers v5.20.1, models/idefics3/modeling_idefics3.py lines 398-407
def pixel_shuffle(self, x, scale_factor=2):
    bsz, seq, embed_dim = x.size()
    height = width = int(seq**0.5)
    x = x.view(bsz, height, width, embed_dim)
    x = x.view(bsz, height, int(width / scale_factor), embed_dim * scale_factor)
    x = x.permute(0, 2, 1, 3)
    x = x.reshape(bsz, int(width / scale_factor), int(height / scale_factor), embed_dim * (scale_factor**2))
    x = x.permute(0, 2, 1, 3)
    x = x.reshape(bsz, int(seq / (scale_factor**2)), embed_dim * (scale_factor**2))
    return x


Other merges do the same job: Qwen2-VL merges 2 × 2 neighbours with an MLP; Gemma 4 pools 3 × 3 (both as the Model map reads their configs). Flamingo’s resampler instead lets 64 learned queries attend to all the features.







3. How many tokens is an image?


The problem. More image tokens let a model see finer detail (small text, a chart’s labels), but each one is a token the language model must attend over, in context and in time. A fixed low resolution (LLaVA-1.5’s one 336-pixel view) misses detail; full resolution at one token per 16-pixel patch would make a 2,048-pixel square 16,384 tokens derived: (2,048 / 16)². Every VLM picks a point between the two.


How SmolVLM does it. Its image processor (transformers v5.20.1, models/idefics3/image_processing_idefics3.py) does three things: it scales the image so its long side equals size.longest_edge (2,048 by default, written N × 512 below with N = 4), keeping the aspect ratio (lines 58–92); it rounds both sides up to whole 512-pixel tiles by resizing, not padding (resize_for_vision_encoder, lines 319–348); and it cuts the tiles and appends the whole image shrunk to 512 as a global view (split_images, lines 286–317). Each view becomes 64 tokens. The processor then writes one placeholder per token into the prompt, with a tag naming each tile’s row and column (processing_idefics3.py lines 216–243).


Three things the counting showed measured


    

  • Input resolution does not change the count. A 64 × 64 icon and a 3,000 × 3,000 photo both become 17 views and 1,088 image tokens: small images are upscaled to 2,048 first. Only the aspect ratio and the N setting matter.
    • 

  • Shapes are stretched to whole tiles. A 1920 × 1080 photo becomes 2,048 × 1,152 and then 2,048 × 1,536 (3 × 4 tiles): height stretched by a third.
    • 

  • N above 6 breaks the tile tags. The vocabulary has <row_1_col_1> to <row_6_col_6> as single learned tokens; <row_7_col_1> is split into 9 ordinary text pieces (<, row, _, 7, ...). At N = 8 a square image takes 4,538 prompt tokens, of which 4,160 are image tokens and 378 are markers.
    • 





Token-budget calculator















    

    The same image in other VLMs derived from configs (read by the Model map; not run here):
    

    

    The calculator re-implements the processor’s arithmetic and reproduces all 36 counts measured with the real processor (the table below) by construction of the same rule, checked by src/vlm/check_calc.mjs. Qwen2-VL’s count is a rough guide: its processor also enforces minimum and maximum pixel limits, ignored here. SmolVLM’s 2.2B sibling uses 384-pixel tiles and 81 tokens per tile (729 patches / 3²; see the Model map); this lab ran the 500M model, with 512-pixel tiles and 64 tokens per tile.
    

    

    All 36 measured counts (the real processor, CPU)
    Question “Describe this image in one sentence.”; prompt tokens include the chat template. Script src/vlm/tokens.py, output out/tokens.json.
    

    Predict, then reveal. You send SmolVLM a 1080 × 1920 phone screenshot. With the default setting, how many image tokens?  832: 1,920 → 2,048 on the long side, 1,080 → 1,152 → rounded up to 1,536, so 4 rows × 3 columns = 12 tiles plus the global view = 13 × 64 measured. Fewer than a 64-pixel icon’s 1,088, because the icon is square.
    

    


    

    4. The prompt the model actually reads
    

    The chat template. A chat model is trained on conversations written in one exact format, its chat template. For a VLM the template also says where the image goes. You write a message with an image and a question; apply_chat_template produces this string, with one <image> placeholder measured:
    

    

    The processor then expands the one placeholder into the tile structure. Runs of <image> are written as <image>x64 here; the real string repeats the token 64 times:
    

    

    

    Where the vectors go. Inside the model the prompt is embedded token by token, and then every <image> position is overwritten, in order, by the projected image vectors:
    

    # transformers v5.20.1, models/idefics3/modeling_idefics3.py lines 557-559 (inputs_merger)
special_image_mask = special_image_mask.unsqueeze(-1).to(inputs_embeds.device)
image_hidden_states = image_hidden_states.to(inputs_embeds.device, inputs_embeds.dtype)
inputs_embeds = inputs_embeds.masked_scatter(special_image_mask, image_hidden_states)
    

    So the language model never sees the placeholder’s own embedding: only its position. If the number of placeholders and the number of image vectors disagree (a hand-written prompt, a processor and model from different versions), the scatter misplaces vectors or fails; always build the prompt with the model’s own processor.
    

    Image tokens are not words. measured The projected image vectors have a median length (L2 norm) of 101 (10th to 90th percentile 83 to 158); the language model’s own word embeddings have a median length of 3.5. The nearest vocabulary embedding to each of the 64 global-view image tokens has a median cosine similarity of 0.27, and the nearest “words” are meaningless: <|im_start|> for 32 of the 64, <|im_end|> for 12, then fragments such as amine. The language model has learned to read these vectors as a different kind of input; they are not disguised words.
    

    The tile tags (<row_1_col_1> and so on) are single learned tokens. The SmolVLM paper found that plain-text position markers “caused early training plateaus” and that “learned positional tokens outperform raw text tokens for compact VLMs” (section 3.1, Finding 5) published; the 9-piece <row_7_col_1> above is exactly the raw-text case.
    

    


    

    5. Training in stages
    

    The problem. The encoder already describes images well and the language model already writes well, but at the start the projector is random: its output vectors mean nothing to the language model. Training everything at once on a little data would let a random projector send noisy gradients into a good language model and damage it.
    

    How it is done. The usual recipe has two stages published:
    

      

    1. Alignment (pretraining the projector). Freeze the encoder and the language model; train only the projector on image-caption pairs, so that image vectors land where the language model can read them. LLaVA used 595K pairs filtered from CC3M with only the projection trained (LLaVA, section 4.2).
      2. 

    2. Instruction tuning. Keep the encoder frozen (usually) and train projector and language model together on conversations about images, so the model learns to answer questions rather than only caption. LLaVA-1.5 used 558K pretraining and 665K instruction samples, “merely 1.2M publicly available data”, in “~1 day on a single 8-A100 node” (Liu et al., October 2023).
      3. 

    

    Later recipes keep this shape and change the details: more and better data (documents, charts, screenshots, synthetic questions), higher resolution with tiling, and often unfreezing the encoder late in training. SmolVLM’s paper says its “training proceeds in two stages: (1) a vision stage, and (2) a video stage”, the video stage keeping “14% of text data and 33% of video” (section 4.1) published; which parts are frozen in each stage is not stated in the passages read for this page.
    

    Not run here, and why. Even the alignment stage of a 500M model needs hundreds of thousands of captioned images and hours of GPU time to show anything; a toy on 16 images would teach memorisation, not alignment. The mechanism is visible without training: the projector is one 960 × 12,288 matrix (11.8M parameters, 2.3% of the model) measured, and stage 1 trains only it.
    

    

    Parameters by component, counted on the loaded model measured. The SmolVLM paper describes the 500M model as “the same 93M SigLIP-B/16 paired with the larger SmolLM2-360M” (section 4) published; the loaded encoder has 86,433,024. The gap is exact arithmetic derived: a SigLIP base vision tower with patch 16 (counted on the Vision lab’s SigLIP 2 base, same architecture) has 92,884,224 parameters, of which 7,087,104 are the attention-pooling head a VLM does not use (it keeps all patch vectors) and 150,528 the position table for 14 × 14 patches; swapping that table for one with 32 × 32 = 1,024 positions (512-pixel input) gives 92,884,224 − 7,087,104 − 150,528 + 786,432 = 86,433,024.
    

    


    

    6. What it gets right and wrong
    

    The question set. 30 questions about the 16 test images with answers known by construction (synthetic images) or checked by eye (photos and generated images): objects, colours, counting, left and right, reading text (OCR, optical character recognition), reading a bar chart, telling the time, and two traps (the cat with a DOG sticker, and the astronaut image whose prompt asked for a horse that Stable Diffusion did not draw). Each was asked at three image-token budgets: one 512-pixel view (64 tokens), 2 × 2 tiles plus the global view (320), and the default 4 × 4 plus global (1,088). Scoring is by pattern match (in src/vlm/qa_set.json) and every answer is shown, so you can judge the scoring.
    

    

    Budget
    

    

    Show
    

    

    

    What the answers show measured. 26 of 30 right at the default 1,088 image tokens, 26 at 320, 24 at 64. The two extra errors at 64 tokens are a count (4 red circles; there are 3) and a chart value (bar C read as 7; it is 5): resolution hurts counting and reading small marks first. Four errors survive every budget: two blue squares counted as 1; the sum of the bars (17; answers 11 or 12), which needs reading four numbers and adding; the clock (1:00 for 3:00, on a face with no numerals); and the puppy’s pose, “sitting”, the word in Stable Diffusion’s prompt, although the generated puppy is lying down: the language prior wins over the image. It read LATENT 42 and STOP exactly, named the cat despite the DOG sticker (and read the sticker), and said the astronaut rides nothing. Median time per answer: 0.22 s, 0.69 s and 2.09 s. Thirty questions is a probe, not a benchmark: one answer is 3.3 points.
    


    Hallucination: asking about things that are not there
    

    The problem. A VLM writes the most likely text given the image and the words so far. When the image is weak evidence, the language model’s habits win: it names objects that usually appear with what is there, or agrees with what the question suggests. This is object hallucination.
    

    How to measure it. POPE (Li et al., May 2023) asks yes/no questions, “Is there a <object> in the image?”, about objects that are present and objects that are absent, the absent ones chosen at random, among frequent objects, or among objects that often co-occur with what is there (adversarial). A model that hallucinates says yes to absent objects. Here: 72 questions, one to two present objects per image, one random absent object, and one or two adversarial ones chosen by hand (a dog for the cat, a horse for the astronaut, numerals on the clock that has none), at two budgets.
    

    

    

    

    All 72 questions and answers
    Budget
    

    

    

    What the probe shows measured. At the default budget 69 of 72 answers are right (95.8%). It says yes to 2 of 47 absent objects, both adversarial: “a dog” on the cat with the DOG sticker (the written word counts as evidence: the typographic attack of the Vision lab reaches the VLM through yes/no questions, although asked “what animal” it says cat), and “a legend” on the bar chart. It says no to one present object, “a red circle” on the shapes image, which it counts correctly when asked how many. With one 64-token view: 68 of 72 (94.4%), yes to 3 absent objects (the dog, the legend, a second hand on the clock), and no to the sticker. Random absent objects: 0 of 16 yes at both budgets. The probe separates random from adversarial objects clearly; with 72 questions it cannot rank the two budgets (one answer is 1.4 points).
    


    Long descriptions drift
    

    Short yes/no answers are one kind of test; a free description is another. Asked to “Describe this image in detail” (up to 120 new tokens), the model’s descriptions are below with claims that are wrong for the image marked (checked by eye against the images; the judgement is this page’s, listed in src/vlm/captions_marks.json).
    

    

    

    What the descriptions show measured. 22 wrong claims in 12 of the 16 descriptions, and every description ran to the 120-token limit (median 3.7 s). The errors sit next to short answers that were right: it read LATENT 42 but describes a blue button with white text; it answered B for the tallest bar but makes A the longest at 7; the clock gains the numerals 1 to 12; the stop sign becomes rectangular. The description of the DOG-sticker image never mentions the sticker. A long answer gives the language model many tokens to fill from its prior once the image evidence is used up; CHAIR (Rohrbach et al., 2018) scores this automatically on captioning sets with object labels, which these images lack, so the marks here are by eye.
    

    


    

    7. Cost per image: time and memory
    

    Where the time goes. Answering a question about an image has three parts: the vision encoder and projector run once per view; prefill runs the language model over the whole prompt once (image tokens included) and fills its key-value cache; decode then produces one token at a time, each reading that cache. More image tokens make the first two dearer and each decoded token a little dearer (a longer cache to read).
    

    

    What the timing shows measured (median of three warm runs, on the cat photo). With the default 17 views, the encoder and projector take 1.61 s and the language model’s prefill of 1,142 tokens 0.44 s; each decoded token then takes 14 ms. With one view (82 prompt tokens) the same steps take 0.11 s and 0.07 s, and 13 ms per token. For short answers the vision encoder is the cost: it runs 17 tiles of 1,024 patches through 12 layers, about 17,400 patch positions against 1,142 language-model positions. Decoding barely changes with the prompt length at this size. Peak GPU memory 2,338 to 2,444 MiB (2.45 to 2.56 GB; the MPS driver’s allocation, sampled every 0.1 s), against the SmolVLM paper’s “1.2GB for the 500M” (section 4.3) published; the paper does not say how it measured, and the MPS driver figure counts everything allocated, so the two are not directly comparable.
    

    What transfers. The token counts, the answers (greedy decoding, bfloat16) and the shape of the trade-off transfer to any machine; the seconds do not. A datacenter GPU runs the encoder and prefill many times faster and batches many images; MPS on an M1 Pro is a laptop GPU sharing memory with the CPU, and these runs were at low priority on a machine shared with other jobs.
    

    


    

    8. Common mistakes and interview questions
    

    Assuming a small image costs few tokens
    SmolVLM upscales to its tile grid: a 64-pixel icon costs the same 1,088 image tokens as a 3,000-pixel photo (section 3). Set size={"longest_edge": N*512} or turn splitting off for small or simple images; measure with the processor, not from the file size.
    

    Writing the prompt by hand
    The placeholders, tile tags and wrappers must match what the model was trained on and the number of image vectors exactly. Use processor.apply_chat_template and then the processor on text and image together; never paste <image> yourself.
    

    Raising resolution past what the model was trained for
    More tiles are not always better: past 6 × 6 SmolVLM’s tile tags stop being single tokens (section 3), and any VLM degrades on token counts and layouts it never saw in training. Check the model card’s recommended settings and measure on your own questions.
    

    Judging a VLM by its captions
    Fluent descriptions hide errors: section 6’s long descriptions add details that are not there. Score with questions that have known answers, including absent objects (POPE-style) and traps, and report the yes rate on absent objects, not only accuracy.
    

    Treating image tokens like words
    Projected image vectors are far from every word embedding (section 4: norms about 30 times larger, nearest vocabulary entries meaningless). Tricks designed for text tokens (pruning by similarity to the vocabulary, reusing text-only quantisation statistics) need checking on image tokens separately.
    

    Forgetting the aspect ratio
    Processors that resize to whole tiles or to a square change the shape of the image (a 16:9 photo stretched by a third here; squashed to a square with splitting off). Thin text and circles suffer first. Pad to a tile-friendly shape yourself if geometry matters.
    

    Interview questions
    

    How does a LLaVA-style VLM turn an image into something the language model reads?
    A ViT encoder makes one vector per patch; a projector (linear or a small MLP), sometimes after merging neighbours, maps each to the language model’s embedding width; those vectors replace image placeholder tokens in the prompt, and the language model attends to them like any token.
    

    Cross-attention (Flamingo) or image tokens (LLaVA): when would you pick each?
    Tokens: simplest, reuse any language model unchanged, best-supported in open tooling; cost is context and attention over every image token. Cross-attention: images do not use context, so many images or long videos are cheaper, and the language model can stay frozen with gates starting at zero; cost is new layers and a less standard model.
    

    Your VLM cannot read small text in screenshots. What do you try?
    More visual tokens where the text is: higher resolution or tiling (more tiles), a smaller merge factor, or cropping to the region; check the processor is not downscaling first; check the aspect ratio is preserved. Then data: OCR-heavy instruction data. Measure the token and latency cost of each.
    

    Why does your VLM hallucinate, and how do you measure it?
    The language model’s prior wins when the visual evidence is weak (low resolution, small objects, co-occurrence habits, leading questions, long generations drifting from the image). Measure with POPE-style yes/no questions on present and absent objects (random, popular, adversarial), report the yes rate on absent objects, and score free descriptions for objects not in the image (CHAIR-style). Mitigate with better grounding data, more image tokens, shorter answers, and refusing when unsure.
    

    Design: a VLM that answers questions about phone screenshots in under one second on a laptop
    Small language model (0.5–2B), SigLIP-class encoder, tiles sized to the screenshot’s aspect ratio, aggressive token merging (pixel shuffle) to keep the prompt near 1,000 tokens, prefix caching of the system prompt, short answers. Here SmolVLM-500M answered a short question about one image in about 2.1 s, 1.6 s of it in the vision encoder on an M1 Pro (section 7), so the budget is the image tokens: count them, then trade tiles for latency on a held-out question set.
    

    What are the two training stages and why freeze anything?
    Stage 1 trains only the projector on captions so image vectors become readable without disturbing the pretrained language model (a random projector would send noise into it); stage 2 instruction-tunes projector and language model on visual conversations. Freezing the encoder saves memory and protects its features; later recipes unfreeze it at a low learning rate.
    

    Scripts, recorded outputs and notes: src/vlm/ in the root’s folder (README.md there says how to rerun everything). Visual ideas built and rejected: src/vlm/viz_ideas.md.

    One prompt, six pipelines: what changed from Stable Diffusion 1.5 to Z-Image
    

    The same text prompt passes through the same four boxes in every open text-to-image model: a text encoder turns words into vectors, a denoiser turns noise into a latent image step by step, guided by those vectors, a scheduler decides the steps, and a VAE decoder turns the latent into pixels. Step through six real pipelines; each box shows its value read from the model's own config files, and what it replaced (struck through). Parameter counts are summed here from the safetensors headers.
    

    Predict first: which box grew the most between 2022 and 2025, the denoiser or the text encoder? Then step through. Switch to VLMs to watch the same kind of change in how an image becomes LLM tokens.

    Which model for which job
    

    Pick a job, a licence need and your hardware. The picker filters the table and ranks what is left: current models first, then newer. Memory is estimated as weights only: parameters times bytes per parameter (2 for bfloat16, 1 for 8-bit, 0.5 for 4-bit), against 75% of the memory you choose, because activations, the text encoder and the VAE need the rest. Treat it as a first filter, not a guarantee.
    

    





    

    

    


    Reading a model licence in one minute
    

    "Open" covers four different things, and the difference decides whether you can ship. Open source in the strict sense means the weights, code and (ideally) data are under an OSI-approved licence such as Apache 2.0 or MIT. Open weights means you can download the weights but the licence may restrict use. Read four clauses:
    

      

    • Field of use: "non-commercial" or "research only" (FLUX.1 [dev], FLUX.2 [dev], Qwen-Image-2.1, Ideogram 4, MusicGen, F5-TTS, XTTS-v2).
      • 

    • Revenue or user thresholds: free until US$1M annual revenue (Stability AI Community License), US$5M (FLUX Kommunity), US$10M (LTX-2.x), or 700 million monthly users (Llama 4), or 1 million visits a month (CogVideoX).
      • 

    • Territory: the Tencent Hunyuan licence "does not apply in the European Union, United Kingdom and South Korea"; Llama 3.2 and Llama 4 withhold multimodal rights from EU-domiciled companies.
      • 

    • Use restrictions and naming: OpenRAIL licences list banned uses; DINOv3 bans military uses and asks for "Built with DINOv3".
      • 

    

    Same family, different licence
    Licences change between versions and sizes: Qwen-Image is Apache 2.0, Qwen-Image-2.1 is research-only; FLUX.2 [klein] 4B is Apache 2.0, the 9B is non-commercial; Gemma 3 used Google's own terms, Gemma 4 is Apache 2.0; DINOv2 is Apache 2.0, DINOv3 has its own licence. Check the licence of the exact checkpoint, not the family. This page summarises; it is not legal advice.
    

    Go deeper: the architectures named here are taught in the Latent lab, Diffusion lab, Flow lab, Vision lab and VLM lab; benchmarks for VLMs live on Long-context and multimodal benchmarks.

    This page
    

    

    Reading
    The whole topic from zero: the five families, latents, diffusion and flow side by side, latent diffusion and DiT, vision encoders, VLMs, native multimodal models, video and audio, evaluation, choosing, mistakes and interview questions. about 30 min, plus 10 for the folded answers and code
    

    Latent lab
    A tiny autoencoder and VAE trained on Fashion-MNIST, the same image through each encoder and decoder, a latent-space explorer, the beta trade-off, codebooks, the Stable Diffusion VAE and its scaling factor. time set when the lab is finished
    

    Diffusion lab
    A tiny class-conditional DDPM, the forward process, schedules, the same noise through 1 to 250 steps with DDPM and DDIM, guidance from 0 to 10, and Stable Diffusion v1.5 for comparison. time set when the lab is finished
    

    Flow lab
    Flow matching on a 2-D toy and on the running example, paths before and after reflow, ODE solvers, flow against diffusion at equal steps. time set when the lab is finished
    

    Vision lab
    Images as patches and tokens, CLIP and SigLIP 2 embeddings, zero-shot classification, similarity matrices, the contrastive loss, a typographic attack. time set when the lab is finished
    

    VLM lab
    SmolVLM taken apart: image tokens at each resolution, the exact prompt, answers with their errors, a hallucination probe, time and memory per image. time set when the lab is finished
    

    Model map
    Image, video and audio generators, vision encoders, VLMs, unified models and libraries with dates, architecture family and licence; a timeline and a picker. time set when the tab is finished
    

    


    Child pages
    

    The Reading tab's Child pages section says what each extends.
    

    

    Autoencoders and VAEs: latents and image tokenizers
    Extends Reading section 2 and the Latent lab. The autoencoder, the VAE and its KL, VQ, FSQ and LFQ quantizers, posterior collapse, and nine pretrained image tokenizers compared on the topic's test images. about 33 min
    

    Diffusion from zero: DDPM, samplers and guidance
    Extends section 3 and the Diffusion lab. DDPM from the forward process up: schedules, prediction targets, samplers from 1 to 1,000 steps, guidance and few-step distillation, on a tiny model and SD 1.5. about 25 min
    

    Flow matching and rectified flow
    Extends section 3 and the Flow lab. The marginal vector field, paths and couplings, reflow, distillation, timestep sampling and the resolution shift, solvers, and production configs. about 32 min
    

    Latent diffusion and diffusion transformers
    Extends section 4. How a text-to-image denoiser is built: why latents, the U-Net, text conditioning, DiT and adaLN-Zero, MMDiT, positions, resolution and cost, with eleven real denoisers counted. about 35 min
    

    Vision encoders: ViT, CLIP and SigLIP
    Extends section 5 and the Vision lab. ViT patches, CLIP and SigLIP compared on the running example, retrieval, tokens and cost. about 26 min
    

    Vision-language models: how images become tokens
    Extends section 6 and the VLM lab. Projectors, tiling and the exact prompt, token and cache budgets, what the model saw, and a hallucination probe. about 25 min
    

    Native multimodal and any-to-any models
    Extends section 7. Fusion designs, discrete and continuous image tokens, autoregressive and masked image generation, unified and any-to-any models, speech in and out, token economics. about 33 min
    

    Video and audio generation
    Extends section 8. Video as space-time patches of a causal VAE latent, full against factorised attention, the published video models, audio as waveforms, spectrograms and codec tokens, codec LMs and flow-matching speech. about 40 min
    

    Evaluating generative models: FID, CLIPScore, preference and VLM benchmarks
    Extends section 9. FID from zero and its sample-count bias, KID, precision and recall, FD-DINOv2 and CMMD, CLIPScore against VQA checks, preference arenas and VLM benchmarks. about 25 min
